title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.

The Oblonsky household was in chaos. The wife had found out that her husband was having an affair with the French girl who had been their family's governess, and she had told him she could not go on living under the same roof with him. Three days had passed in this state, and the husband, the wife, every member of the family and every servant in the house was painfully aware of it. Everyone in the house felt that there was no point in their living together, that strangers thrown together by accident at any wayside inn had more in common with each other than they — the family and staff of the Oblonskys — had with one another. The wife stayed shut in her room; the husband had not been home for three days. The children ran wild through the house; the English governess had quarreled with the housekeeper and had written to a friend asking her to look out for a new position; the cook had walked out yesterday in the middle of dinner; the kitchen-maid and the coachman had given notice.

Three days after the quarrel, Prince Stepan Arkadyevitch Oblonsky — Stiva, as fashionable society called him — woke at his usual hour, eight in the morning, but not in his wife's bedroom: on the leather sofa in his study. He rolled his plump, well-groomed body over on the springy cushions as if he meant to slip back into a long sleep, threw his arms around the pillow on the other side and pressed his face into it; then suddenly he jumped, sat up on the sofa, and opened his eyes.

"Yes, yes, how did it go now?" he thought, going back over his dream. "How was it? Right — Alabin was giving a dinner in Darmstadt; no, not Darmstadt, somewhere American. Yes, but in the dream Darmstadt was in America. So Alabin was giving a dinner on glass tables, and the tables were singing _Il mio tesoro_ — only not exactly _Il mio tesoro_, something better — and there were these little decanters standing on the table, and the decanters were women, too," he remembered.

Stepan Arkadyevitch's eyes twinkled with amusement, and he thought it over with a smile. "Yes, it was lovely, really lovely. There was a great deal more that was charming, only you can't put it into words, or even pin it down in your thoughts once you're awake." Noticing a thin band of daylight slipping in past the edge of one of the serge curtains, he swung his feet cheerfully off the sofa and felt around for the slippers his wife had embroidered for his last birthday in gold-stitched morocco. And then, as he had done every morning for the past nine years, without getting up he reached out for the spot in his bedroom where his dressing-gown always hung. And it was at that point that he suddenly remembered he was not sleeping in his wife's room but in his study, and remembered why; the smile vanished from his face, and he frowned.

"Ugh, ugh, ugh! Oh..." he muttered, the whole quarrel rushing back. Every detail of the row with his wife came up again in his mind, the hopelessness of the situation, and — worst of all — that the fault was entirely his.

"She won't forgive me, and she can't forgive me. And the most awful part of it is that it's all my fault — all my fault, even though I'm not really to blame. That's the whole point of the situation," he reflected. "Oh, oh, oh!" he kept repeating in despair as the sharp pain of the quarrel came back over him.

The worst of it had been that first moment when he came home from the theater, happy and good-humored, with an enormous pear in his hand for his wife, and could not find her in the drawing-room, and to his surprise did not find her in his study either, and finally found her in her bedroom, holding in her hand the unlucky letter that had given everything away.

She — his Dolly, forever fussing and worrying over household details, narrow-minded, as he considered her — was sitting completely still with the letter in her hand, staring at him with an expression of horror, despair, and outrage.
"What is this? This?" she had asked, pointing at the letter.
And remembering it now, Stepan Arkadyevitch — as so often happens — was less upset by the thing itself than by the way he had handled what his wife said.

Something happened to him at that instant that happens to people when they are caught unexpectedly in something disgraceful. He could not get his face to match the position he had been put in by the discovery of his fault. Instead of being hurt, denying it, defending himself, begging forgiveness — instead even of being coolly indifferent, anything would have been better than what he did — his face, completely involuntarily (a reflex of the spinal cord, Stepan Arkadyevitch reflected, having a taste for physiology), completely involuntarily, settled into its usual good-natured and therefore idiotic smile.

That idiotic smile he could not forgive himself. When Dolly caught sight of it she shuddered as if at a stab of physical pain, broke out, with her usual fire, into a stream of cruel words, and ran out of the room. Since then she had refused to see him.
"It's that idiotic smile that's to blame for everything," Stepan Arkadyevitch thought.
"But what's to be done? What's to be done?" he kept asking himself in despair, and he could find no answer.

title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch was an honest man with himself. He was incapable of fooling himself into thinking he was sorry for what he had done. He could not, at this stage in his life, be sorry that he, a handsome and susceptible man of thirty-four, was no longer in love with his wife — the mother of five living and two dead children, and only a year younger than he was. All he was sorry about was that he had not done a better job of hiding it from her. But he felt the full weight of his situation, and was sorry for his wife, for his children, and for himself. Perhaps he could have managed to keep his affairs better hidden from her if he had foreseen how badly the discovery would hit her. He had never thought it through clearly, but he had vaguely supposed that his wife must have suspected him of being unfaithful long ago and had chosen to look the other way. He had even assumed that she — a worn-out woman, no longer young or pretty, in no way striking or interesting, a good mother and nothing more — ought, out of basic fairness, to take a tolerant view of it. It had turned out exactly the opposite.

"Oh, it's awful! Oh dear, oh dear, awful!" Stepan Arkadyevitch kept saying to himself, and he could not think of anything to do. "And how well things were going up till now! How well we got along! She was content, happy in her children; I never got in her way over anything; I let her run the children and the house however she liked. It's true that the girl having been _our_ governess in the house was bad. That's bad! There is something cheap and vulgar about flirting with one's governess. But what a governess she was!" (He vividly recalled the mischievous black eyes of Mlle. Roland, and her smile.) "But still, while she was in the house I kept myself in check. And the worst of it now is that she's already... it's just bad luck that it had to turn out this way! Oh, oh! But what, what is to be done?"

There was no real answer, except the universal answer life gives to every question, even the most tangled and unanswerable. That answer is: live in the day-to-day — that is, forget yourself. To forget himself in sleep was impossible now, at least till nighttime; he could not slip back into the music sung by the decanter-women; so he would have to forget himself in the routine of daily life.

"We'll see, then," Stepan Arkadyevitch said to himself, and getting up he pulled on a gray dressing-gown lined with blue silk, knotted its tassels, drew a deep breath into his broad bare chest, and walked to the window with his usual confident step, his feet turned out in the easy way that carried his full frame so lightly. He yanked up the blind and rang the bell sharply. Almost at once Matvey, his old valet and friend, came in with his clothes, his boots, and a telegram. Behind Matvey came the barber with everything needed for shaving.
"Anything from the office?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked, taking the telegram and sitting down at the looking-glass.
"On the table," Matvey said, glancing at his master with sympathetic curiosity; and after a brief pause he added with a sly little smile, "They've sent from the carriage hire."

Stepan Arkadyevitch did not answer, only glanced at Matvey in the mirror. From the look that passed between them in the glass it was clear they understood each other perfectly. Stepan Arkadyevitch's glance asked: "Why bring that up? Don't you know how things stand?"
Matvey stuck his hands in his jacket pockets, planted one foot out, and stood looking at his master in silence, good-humored, with the faintest smile.
"I told them to come back on Sunday, and till then not to bother you or themselves for nothing," he said. He had obviously rehearsed the line in advance.

Stepan Arkadyevitch saw that Matvey was setting up a joke and angling for attention. Tearing open the telegram, he read it through, guessing at the misspellings telegrams always have, and his face lit up.
"Matvey, my sister Anna Arkadyevna is arriving tomorrow," he said, briefly checking the smooth, plump hand of the barber, which was carving a pink path through his long curly whiskers.

"Thank God!" said Matvey — making clear by his response that, like his master, he understood the significance of the visit: that Anna Arkadyevna, the sister Stepan Arkadyevitch was so fond of, might bring about a reconciliation between him and his wife.
"Alone, or with her husband?" Matvey asked.
Stepan Arkadyevitch could not speak — the barber was working on his upper lip — and held up one finger. Matvey nodded back at him in the mirror.
"Alone. Should the upstairs room be made ready?"
"Ask Darya Alexandrovna; whatever she decides."
"Darya Alexandrovna?" Matvey repeated, as if uncertain.
"Yes, ask her. Here, take the telegram, give it to her, and do whatever she says."
"You want to feel her out," Matvey understood, but all he said was, "Yes, sir."

Stepan Arkadyevitch had already washed and combed his hair and was waiting to be dressed when Matvey came back into the room, stepping carefully in his creaky boots, the telegram in his hand. The barber had gone.

"Darya Alexandrovna told me to inform you she's leaving. Let him do — that is, you — as he likes," he said, his eyes alone laughing as he tucked his hands into his pockets and watched his master, his head tipped to one side. Stepan Arkadyevitch was quiet for a moment. Then a good-humored, slightly pitiful smile crossed his handsome face.
"Well, Matvey?" he said, shaking his head.
"It's all right, sir; she'll come round," said Matvey.
"Come round?"
"Yes, sir."
"Do you think so? Who's there?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked, hearing the rustle of a woman's dress at the door.
"It's me," said a firm, pleasant woman's voice, and the stern, pockmarked face of Matrona Philimonovna, the nurse, appeared in the doorway.
"Well, what is it, Matrona?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked, going up to her at the door.

Although Stepan Arkadyevitch was completely in the wrong with regard to his wife, and knew it himself, almost everyone in the house — even the nurse, Darya Alexandrovna's chief ally — was on his side.
"Well, what now?" he asked dejectedly.

"Go to her, sir, and admit your fault again. Maybe God will help you. She's suffering so, it's terrible to see; the whole house is upside down. You've got to think of the children, sir. Beg her forgiveness. There's no other way. You have to face what you've done..."
"But she won't see me."
"You do your part. God is merciful; pray to God, sir, pray to God."
"All right, that's enough, you can go," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, blushing suddenly. "Now, dress me." He turned to Matvey and threw off the dressing-gown with decision.
Matvey was already holding up the shirt like a horse's collar, and, blowing off some invisible speck, he slipped it with obvious satisfaction over his master's well-groomed body.

title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: Once he was dressed, Stepan Arkadyevitch sprinkled some scent on himself, pulled down his shirt-cuffs, distributed his cigarettes, wallet, matches and watch with its double chain and seals into his pockets, shook out his handkerchief, and feeling clean, fragrant, healthy, and physically at ease in spite of his unhappiness, he walked, with the slight swing in each leg that was his trademark, into the dining-room, where coffee was already waiting for him, and beside the coffee, his letters and papers from the office.

He read the letters. One was very unpleasant — from a merchant who was buying a wood on his wife's estate. Selling that wood was absolutely necessary, but at the moment, until he and his wife were reconciled, the subject could not even be raised. What was most unpleasant of all was that his financial interests should be mixed up in this way with the question of making things up with his wife. The idea that he might be driven by self-interest — that he might be seeking a reconciliation with his wife on account of the sale of a wood — pained him.

Having gone through the letters, Stepan Arkadyevitch pulled the office papers over to him, ran quickly through two cases, made a few notes with a large pencil, pushed the papers away again and turned to his coffee. As he drank, he opened a still-damp morning newspaper and started to read.

Stepan Arkadyevitch took and read a liberal paper — not an extreme one, but one representing the views held by the majority. And although he had no real personal interest in science, art, or politics, he firmly held the views on all of them that the majority and his paper held, and he changed them only when the majority changed them — or rather, he did not change them; they changed inside him imperceptibly, of their own accord.

Stepan Arkadyevitch had not chosen his political opinions or his views; these political opinions and views had come to him on their own, just as he did not choose the cut of his hat or his coat but simply took whatever was being worn. And for him, living in the kind of society he lived in — given the ordinary mental restlessness that comes with adulthood — having views was just as indispensable as having a hat. If there was a reason he preferred liberal opinions to the conservative ones held by many in his circle, it was not because he considered liberalism more rational, but because it fit better with the way he lived. The liberal party said that everything in Russia was wrong, and certainly Stepan Arkadyevitch had plenty of debts and was decidedly short of cash. The liberal party said that marriage was an outdated institution that needed reform; and family life certainly gave Stepan Arkadyevitch very little pleasure, and forced him into lies and hypocrisy, which his nature found repulsive. The liberal party said, or at least implied, that religion was only a check kept on the lower orders; and Stepan Arkadyevitch couldn't get through even a short church service without his legs aching from standing, and could never figure out what was the point of all the dire and lofty talk about another world when life in this one might be so very amusing. And besides, Stepan Arkadyevitch, who liked a joke, was fond of teasing solid citizens by saying that if a man was going to take pride in his lineage he should not stop at Rurik but should not disown the original founder of the family — the ape. So Liberalism had become a habit with Stepan Arkadyevitch, and he liked his newspaper, the way he liked his cigar after dinner, for the slight fog it spread through his brain. He read the leading article, which argued that in our day it was simply silly to raise an outcry that radicalism was about to swallow up every conservative element, and that the government ought to take steps to crush the revolutionary hydra; on the contrary, "in our opinion the danger lies not in this imaginary revolutionary hydra, but in the stubbornness of traditionalism choking off progress," and so on, and so on. He read another article, a financial one, which alluded to Bentham and Mill and slipped in some innuendoes aimed at the ministry. With his quick wit he caught the drift of each innuendo, guessed where it came from, who it was aimed at and on what grounds, and that gave him, as it always did, a certain satisfaction. But today the satisfaction was spoiled by the memory of Matrona Philimonovna's advice and the unhappy state of the house. He also read that Count Beist was rumored to have left for Wiesbaden, and that there was no need ever to have gray hair again, and that a light carriage was for sale, and that a young person was looking for a position; but these items did not give him the quiet, ironical pleasure they usually did. Having finished the paper, a second cup of coffee, and a buttered roll, he got up, shook the crumbs off his waistcoat, and, squaring his broad chest, smiled with sheer pleasure: not because anything in particular had pleased him, but because his digestion was good.
But that smile of pure pleasure brought everything back to him at once, and he turned grave.

Two childish voices (Stepan Arkadyevitch recognized them as belonging to Grisha, his younger boy, and Tanya, his oldest girl) were heard outside the door. They were carrying something, and it crashed to the floor.
"I told you not to put passengers on the roof," the little girl said in English; "now, pick them up!"

"Everything's in chaos," Stepan Arkadyevitch thought; "now the children are running loose." He went to the door and called them. They dropped the box, which was meant to be a train, and came in to their father.

The little girl, her father's favorite, ran up boldly, hugged him, and hung laughing on his neck, enjoying as always the scent that came from his whiskers. At last she kissed his face — flushed from his stooping, beaming with tenderness — let go of him, and was about to run off again; but her father held her back.

"How is mamma?" he asked, running his hand over his daughter's smooth, soft little neck. "Good morning," he said, smiling at the boy, who had come up to say hello. He was aware that he loved the boy less, and always tried to be fair; but the boy felt it, and did not smile back at his father's cool smile.
"Mamma? She's up," answered the girl.
Stepan Arkadyevitch sighed. "Which means she hasn't slept again all night," he thought.
"Well, is she in good spirits?"

The little girl knew there had been a quarrel between her father and her mother, and that her mother could not be in good spirits, and that her father must know it, and was pretending when he asked so casually. And she blushed for him. He noticed at once, and blushed too.
"I don't know," she said. "She didn't tell us we had to do our lessons, but she said we should walk over to grandmamma's with Miss Hoole."
"Well, run along, Tanya darling. Oh, wait a moment, though," he said, still holding her and stroking her soft little hand.
From the mantelpiece, where he had left it the day before, he took down a small box of sweets and handed her two — picking out the ones she liked best, a chocolate and a fondant.
"For Grisha?" the little girl said, pointing to the chocolate.
"Yes, yes." Still stroking her little shoulder, he kissed her on the roots of her hair and on her neck, and let her go.
"The carriage is ready," said Matvey; "and there's someone here to see you with a petition."
"Has he been here long?" asked Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Half an hour."
"How many times have I told you to let me know at once?"
"A man has to be allowed to drink his coffee in peace," Matvey said, in the gruff-but-affectionate tone it was impossible to be angry with.
"Well, send him up at once," said Oblonsky, frowning with annoyance.

The petitioner — the widow of a staff-captain named Kalinin — had come with a request that was impossible and unreasonable. But Stepan Arkadyevitch, as was his habit, made her sit down, listened to her right through without interrupting, gave her detailed advice on how and to whom to apply, and even wrote her, in his large, sprawling, neat and legible hand, a confident, fluent little note to an influential person who might be of use to her. Having sent the staff-captain's widow on her way, Stepan Arkadyevitch picked up his hat and paused to think whether he had forgotten anything. It turned out he had forgotten nothing — except what he wanted to forget: his wife.

"Ah, yes." He hung his head, and his handsome face took on a harassed look. "To go, or not to go?" he said to himself; and an inner voice told him not to go, that nothing could come of it but falsity; that to repair, to put right their relations, was impossible, because it was impossible to make her attractive again, able to inspire love, or to turn him into an old man no longer susceptible to love. Nothing could come of it now except deceit and lying — and deceit and lying went against his nature.

"Still, it has to happen sometime; we can't go on like this," he said, trying to nerve himself. He squared his chest, took out a cigarette, drew two puffs from it, tossed it into a mother-of-pearl ashtray, and with quick steps walked across the drawing-room and opened the other door into his wife's bedroom.

title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: Darya Alexandrovna, in a dressing jacket, her once thick and beautiful hair now thin and pinned up at the back of her neck, her face sunken and gaunt, her large startled eyes made all the more prominent by the thinness of her face, was standing in the middle of the room amid a clutter of things scattered everywhere, in front of an open bureau from which she was taking something out. When she heard her husband's footsteps she stopped, looked toward the door, and made a determined effort to set her features into a stern, contemptuous expression. She felt afraid of him, and afraid of the interview ahead. She was just trying to do what she had attempted ten times in the last three days — sort out the children's things and her own, so as to take them to her mother's — and once again she could not bring herself to do it; but again, as each time before, she kept telling herself that things could not go on this way, that she had to do something to punish him, shame him, take some small revenge for the suffering he had inflicted on her. She kept telling herself she would leave him, but in her heart she knew it was impossible — impossible because she could not get out of the habit of regarding him as her husband and loving him. Besides, she realized that if even here, in her own home, she could barely manage to look after her five children properly, they would be still worse off wherever she took them. As it was, in just these three days the youngest had already been unwell from being given bad soup, and the others had almost gone without their dinner the day before. She knew it was impossible to go away; but, deceiving herself, she went on sorting out her things and pretending she was going.

When she saw her husband, she dropped her hands into the drawer of the bureau as if looking for something, and only turned around when he was already up beside her. But the face she tried to set into a stern and resolute expression betrayed her bewilderment and pain.

"Dolly!" he said in a quiet, timid voice. He bent his head toward his shoulder and tried to look pitiful and humble, but in spite of himself he was glowing with freshness and health. In one quick glance she took in his figure, beaming with health and freshness. "Yes, he's happy and content!" she thought, "while I... And that disgusting good nature, which everyone likes him for and praises — I hate that good nature of his." Her mouth set hard, and the muscles in her right cheek tightened on her pale, nervous face.
"What do you want?" she said in a quick, deep, unnatural voice.
"Dolly!" he said again, his voice catching. "Anna is arriving today."
"Well, what is that to me? I can't see her!" she cried.
"But you must, really, Dolly..."
"Go away, go away, go away!" she shrieked, not looking at him, as if the shriek had been wrenched out of her by physical pain.

Stepan Arkadyevitch could be calm when he merely thought about his wife, could hope that she would _come round_, as Matvey put it, and could go on quietly reading his paper and drinking his coffee; but when he saw her tortured, suffering face, when he heard her voice, with its tone of submission to fate and full of despair, his breath caught, there was a lump in his throat, and his eyes began to fill with tears.
"My God! What have I done? Dolly! For God's sake!... You know..." He couldn't go on; a sob was rising in his throat.
She slammed the bureau shut and looked at him.
"Dolly, what can I say? One thing: forgive me. Remember — can't nine years of my life make up for a single moment of..."
She dropped her eyes and listened, waiting to hear what he would say, as if begging him somehow to convince her otherwise.
"— a moment of passion?" he said, and would have continued, but at that word, as at a pang of physical pain, her lips tightened again, and the muscles in her right cheek twitched again.
"Go away, get out of this room!" she shrieked, more shrilly than before, "and don't talk to me about your passion and your filth."
She tried to leave the room but staggered and caught hold of the back of a chair to steady herself. His face crumpled, his lips swelled, his eyes filled with tears.

"Dolly!" he said, sobbing now. "For pity's sake, think of the children — they aren't to blame. I am to blame. Punish me, make me atone. Anything you ask, I'll do — anything! I'm to blame, no words can say how much. But, Dolly, forgive me!"
She sat down. He listened to her heavy, ragged breathing, and felt unspeakably sorry for her. She tried several times to begin to speak and could not. He waited.

"You remember the children, Stiva, in order to play with them; but I remember them, and I know what this means for them — that it will ruin them," she said — clearly one of the lines she had repeated to herself many times over the past few days.
She had called him "Stiva," and he glanced at her gratefully and moved to take her hand, but she pulled it away in disgust.

"I think of the children, and that's why I'd do anything in the world to save them — but I don't know how to save them myself. By taking them away from their father, or by leaving them with a vicious father — yes, a vicious father... Tell me, after what... has happened, can we live together? Is that possible? Tell me, is it possible?" she repeated, her voice rising, "after my husband, the father of my children, has had an affair with his own children's governess?"
"But what was I supposed to do? What was I supposed to do?" he kept repeating in a pitiful voice, scarcely aware of what he was saying, his head dropping lower and lower.

"You are loathsome to me, repulsive!" she shrieked, getting more and more worked up. "Your tears mean nothing! You never loved me; you have no heart, no decency! You are hateful to me, disgusting, a stranger — yes, a complete stranger!" With pain and fury she pronounced the word she found so terrible — _stranger_.

He looked at her, and the fury in her face alarmed and astonished him. He didn't understand how his pity for her could make her so much angrier. She saw in him sympathy, but not love. "No, she hates me. She'll never forgive me," he thought.
"This is awful! Awful!" he said.
Just then, in the next room, a child started to cry — probably from a fall. Darya Alexandrovna listened, and her face softened all at once.
For a few seconds she seemed to gather herself, as if she didn't know where she was or what she was doing, and then she rose quickly and moved toward the door.
"Well, she loves my child," he thought, noticing the change in her face at the sound of the crying, "my child — how can she hate me?"
"Dolly, one more word," he said, following her.
"If you come near me, I'll call the servants and the children! Let them all know you're a scoundrel! I'm leaving right now, and you can live here with your mistress!"
And she went out, slamming the door.

Stepan Arkadyevitch sighed, wiped his face, and walked softly out of the room. "Matvey says she'll come round; but how? I don't see the slightest chance. Oh, oh, how horrible it is! And how vulgarly she shouted," he said to himself, remembering her shriek and the words "scoundrel" and "mistress." "And very likely the maids heard! Horribly vulgar, horrible!" Stepan Arkadyevitch stood a few seconds alone, wiped his face, squared his chest, and walked out.

It was Friday, and in the dining-room the German watchmaker was winding the clock. Stepan Arkadyevitch remembered his joke about this punctual, bald watchmaker — "that the German himself was wound up for a lifetime to wind up watches" — and smiled. Stepan Arkadyevitch was fond of a joke. "And maybe she will come round! That's a good expression, _come round_," he thought. "I must use that again."
"Matvey!" he called. "Sort everything out with Darya in the sitting-room for Anna Arkadyevna," he said when Matvey came in.
"Yes, sir."
Stepan Arkadyevitch pulled on his fur coat and walked out onto the front steps.
"You won't be dining at home?" Matvey asked, seeing him off.
"We'll see how it goes. Here's something for the housekeeping," he said, taking ten roubles out of his wallet. "That should be enough."
"Enough or not, we'll have to make it do," said Matvey, slamming the carriage door and stepping back onto the porch.

Darya Alexandrovna, meanwhile, having calmed the child, and knowing from the sound of the carriage that her husband had gone, went back to her bedroom. It was her one refuge from the household troubles that came crowding in on her the moment she stepped out of it. Even now, in the short time she had been in the nursery, the English governess and Matrona Philimonovna had managed to put several questions to her that could not wait and that only she could answer: what should the children wear for their walk? Should they have any milk? Shouldn't they send for a new cook?

"Oh, let me alone, let me alone!" she said, and going back to her bedroom she sat down in the same spot where she had sat while talking with her husband. She clasped her thin hands tightly together, the rings sliding down on her bony fingers, and went back over the whole conversation in her mind. "He's gone! But has he broken it off with her?" she thought. "Could he still be seeing her? Why didn't I ask him? No, no, reconciliation is impossible. Even if we go on living in the same house, we are strangers — strangers forever!" She repeated the word she found so dreadful with deliberate weight. "And how I loved him! My God, how I loved him!... How I loved him! And now — don't I love him? Don't I love him more than ever? The most horrible thing is —" she began, but did not finish, because Matrona Philimonovna stuck her head in at the door.
"Let's send for my brother," she said. "At least he can put together a dinner, or the children will go without till six again, like yesterday."
"Very well, I'll come and see to it in a minute. But did you send for some new milk?"
And Darya Alexandrovna plunged into the duties of the day, and for a while she drowned her grief in them.

title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: Stepan Arkadyevitch had got through school easily, thanks to his excellent abilities, but he had been lazy and mischievous and so had finished near the bottom of his class. Yet in spite of his habitually dissipated way of life, his modest official rank, and his comparative youth, he held the respectable and lucrative position of head of one of the government boards in Moscow. This post he had got through his sister Anna's husband, Alexey Alexandrovitch Karenin, who held one of the most important positions in the ministry that the Moscow office belonged to. But even if Karenin had not arranged the position for his brother-in-law, then through any of a hundred other contacts — brothers, sisters, cousins, uncles, and aunts — Stiva Oblonsky would have got this post, or some similar one, along with the six thousand a year that was indispensable to him, since his affairs, in spite of his wife's considerable fortune, were in an embarrassed state.

Half of Moscow and Petersburg were friends or relations of Stepan Arkadyevitch. He had been born among the people who had been and still were the powers of this world. One-third of the men in government, the older men, had been friends of his father's and had known him in baby clothes; another third were his close friends, and the rest were friendly acquaintances. So the distributors of earthly goods — in the form of posts, leases, shares, and the like — were all his friends, and could not overlook one of their own; and Oblonsky did not have to make any particular effort to get a lucrative position. He simply had not to refuse anything, not to show envy, not to be quarrelsome or take offense, all of which his easygoing nature kept him from doing anyway. It would have struck him as absurd if he had been told that he would not get a position with the salary he needed, especially since he was not asking for anything out of the ordinary; he wanted only what the men of his age and standing got, and he was no less qualified to do that kind of work than anyone else.

Stepan Arkadyevitch was liked by everyone who knew him not only for his good humor but also for his sunny temper and his unquestionable honesty. There was something in him, in his handsome, glowing figure, his bright eyes, black hair and eyebrows, and the white and red of his face, that gave people who met him an almost physical sense of warmth and good cheer. "Aha! Stiva! Oblonsky! There he is!" was nearly always said with a smile of pleasure on meeting him. And even if, sometimes, after a conversation with him it turned out that nothing particularly delightful had actually happened, the next day, and the day after, everyone was just as pleased to see him again.

For three years, as head of one of the Moscow government boards, Stepan Arkadyevitch had earned the respect as well as the affection of his colleagues, subordinates, superiors, and everyone who had dealings with him. The chief qualities in Stepan Arkadyevitch that had won him this universal respect in the service were, first, his great tolerance toward others, founded on his awareness of his own shortcomings; second, his perfect liberalism — not the liberalism he read about in the newspapers, but the kind in his blood, which made him treat all men exactly the same, whatever their wealth or station; and third — and most important — his complete indifference to the business he was engaged in, in consequence of which he never got carried away and never made mistakes.

Arriving at the offices of the board, Stepan Arkadyevitch, escorted by a deferential porter carrying his portfolio, went into his small private room, put on his uniform, and walked into the boardroom. The clerks and copyists all rose, greeting him with friendly respect. Stepan Arkadyevitch moved quickly, as always, to his place, shook hands with his colleagues, and sat down. He made a joke or two and chatted just enough to stay within the bounds of proper decorum, and got down to work. No one was better than Stepan Arkadyevitch at finding the exact balance between ease, simplicity, and official correctness needed to keep business running pleasantly. A secretary, with the easy good humor everyone in Stepan Arkadyevitch's office had picked up from him, came up with some papers and began to speak in the familiar, casual tone Stepan Arkadyevitch had introduced.
"We've managed to get the information from the Penza government department. Here, would you like to...?"
"You've finally got them?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, laying his finger on the paper. "Now, gentlemen..."
And the session of the board began.

"If they knew," he thought, bowing his head with an air of significance as he listened to the report, "what a guilty little boy their president was half an hour ago." And his eyes were laughing as the report was read. The session would run without a break until two o'clock, when there would be an interval for lunch.
It was not yet two when the large glass doors of the boardroom suddenly swung open and someone walked in.

All the officials sitting at the far end of the room beneath the portrait of the Tsar and the eagle, delighted at any distraction, looked toward the door; but the doorkeeper standing there at once steered the intruder out and shut the glass door behind him.

When the case had been read through, Stepan Arkadyevitch got up and stretched, and, by way of a tribute to the liberalism of the age, took out a cigarette in the boardroom and went into his private office. Two of the board members, the veteran in the service Nikitin and the _Kammerjunker_ Grinevitch, went in with him.
"We'll have time to finish after lunch," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"To be sure we will," said Nikitin.
"This Fomin must be a fairly sharp fellow," said Grinevitch, of one of the parties in the case they were looking at.
Stepan Arkadyevitch frowned at Grinevitch's remark, conveying that it was not proper to pass judgment prematurely, and gave him no reply.
"Who was that who came in?" he asked the doorkeeper.
"Someone slipped in without permission, your excellency, the moment my back was turned. He was asking for you. I told him: not till the members come out..."
"Where is he?"

"Maybe he's gone out into the passage, but here he is now. That's him," said the doorkeeper, pointing to a powerfully built, broad-shouldered man with a curly beard, who, without taking off his sheepskin cap, was running quickly and lightly up the worn steps of the stone staircase. One of the members coming down — a thin official with a portfolio — stepped out of his way, looked disapprovingly at the stranger's legs, and then glanced inquiringly at Oblonsky.

Stepan Arkadyevitch was standing at the top of the staircase. The good-natured glow on his face, framed by the embroidered collar of his uniform, broke into something brighter still the moment he recognized the man coming up.

"Why, it's actually you, Levin, at last!" he said with a warm, mocking smile, looking him over as he approached. "How is it you've deigned to come and find me in this den?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch — and not content with shaking hands, he kissed his friend. "Have you been in town long?"
"I've just arrived, and I very much wanted to see you," said Levin, looking around shyly and at the same time uneasily and angrily.
"Well, let's go into my room," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, who knew his friend's touchy, irritable shyness, and, taking his arm, he steered him along, as if guiding him through dangers.

Stepan Arkadyevitch was on first-name terms with nearly all his acquaintances and called nearly all of them by their Christian names: old men of sixty, boys of twenty, actors, ministers, merchants, adjutant generals — so that many of his intimate friends were to be found at opposite ends of the social ladder, and would have been very surprised to learn that, through Oblonsky, they had anything in common. He was the familiar friend of everyone with whom he had had a glass of champagne, and he had a glass of champagne with everyone, and when, in consequence, he happened to run into any of his disreputable cronies (as he jokingly called many of his friends) in front of his subordinates, he knew exactly how, with his characteristic tact, to soften any awkward impression. Levin was no disreputable crony, but Oblonsky, with his ready tact, sensed that Levin might be uncomfortable having his familiarity with him displayed in front of his subordinates, and so he hurried to whisk him into his private room.

Levin was almost the same age as Oblonsky; their friendship did not rest on champagne alone. Levin had been the friend and companion of his early youth. They were fond of each other in spite of the difference in their characters and tastes, the way friends are fond of one another after sharing a youth together. But in spite of this, each of them — as so often happens with men who have chosen very different careers — though in conversation he would even defend the other's path, secretly looked down on it. Each of them thought the life he himself led was the only real life and that the life led by his friend was just an illusion. Oblonsky could not suppress a slight mocking smile at the sight of Levin. He had seen him come up to Moscow from the country many times, where he was doing something — though what exactly Stepan Arkadyevitch could never quite make out, and in fact took no interest in. Levin would arrive in Moscow always agitated and in a rush, rather awkward and irritated by his own awkwardness, and almost always with some perfectly new, unexpected view of things. Stepan Arkadyevitch laughed at this, and liked it. In the same way Levin in his heart looked down on his friend's town way of life and his official duties, which he laughed at and regarded as trifling. The difference was that Oblonsky, since he was doing what everyone else did, laughed about it complacently and good-humoredly, whereas Levin laughed without complacency, and sometimes angrily.

"We've been expecting you for ages," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, going into his room and letting go of Levin's hand as if to show that here the danger was over. "I'm very, very glad to see you," he went on. "So, how are you? When did you get in?"

Levin was silent, staring at the unfamiliar faces of Oblonsky's two companions, especially the hand of the elegant Grinevitch, with such long white fingers, such long yellow filbert-shaped nails, and such huge gleaming studs on the shirt-cuff, that it seemed to absorb all his attention and leave him no room to think. Oblonsky noticed at once and smiled.

"Ah, of course — let me introduce you," he said. "My colleagues: Philip Ivanitch Nikitin, Mihail Stanislavitch Grinevitch" — and turning to Levin — "a district councilor, a modern district councilman, a gymnast who can lift thirteen stone with one hand, a cattle-breeder and sportsman, and my friend Konstantin Dmitrievitch Levin, the brother of Sergey Ivanovitch Koznishev."
"Delighted," said the veteran.
"I have the honor of knowing your brother, Sergey Ivanovitch," said Grinevitch, holding out his slender, long-nailed hand.

Levin frowned, shook hands coldly, and turned at once to Oblonsky. Though he had a great deal of respect for his half-brother, a writer known all over Russia, he could not stand being treated not as Konstantin Levin, but as the brother of the celebrated Koznishev.
"No, I'm no longer a district councilor. I've quarreled with the lot of them and don't go to the meetings anymore," he said, turning to Oblonsky.
"That was quick!" said Oblonsky with a smile. "But how? Why?"

"It's a long story. I'll tell you sometime," said Levin — but he started telling him right away. "Well, in short: I became convinced that nothing was really being done by the district councils, and nothing ever could be," he began, as if someone had just insulted him. "On one side it's a plaything — they play at being a parliament, and I'm neither young enough nor old enough to find amusement in playthings; and on the other side" (he stammered) "it's a way for the local clique to make money. They used to have wardships and courts of justice; now they have the district council — not in the form of bribes, but as unearned salary," he said, as heatedly as if someone present had argued the opposite.
"Aha! You're in a new phase again, I see — a conservative," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "But we can go into all that later."
"Yes, later. But I wanted to see you," said Levin, looking with loathing at Grinevitch's hand.
Stepan Arkadyevitch gave the faintest of smiles.
"Wasn't it you who used to say you'd never wear European dress again?" he said, looking over his new suit, obviously cut by a French tailor. "Ah! I see: a new phase."

Levin suddenly blushed, not the way grown men blush, faintly, without being aware of it, but the way boys blush — feeling that they're being ridiculous out of shyness, and so ashamed of it that they blush still more, almost to the point of tears. And it was so strange to see this sensible, manly face in such a boyish state that Oblonsky looked away.
"Where shall we meet, then? You know I really want to talk with you," said Levin.
Oblonsky appeared to think it over.
"I'll tell you what: let's go to Gurin's for lunch and talk there. I'm free till three."
"No," Levin answered after a moment's thought, "I have to go somewhere else."
"All right then, let's have dinner together."
"Dinner together? But there's nothing in particular I want to say — just a few words, and a question I want to ask you, and we can have a real talk afterward."
"Well, say the few words now, then, and we'll chat over dinner."
"All right, it's this," Levin said; "but it's not important, really."
His face suddenly took on an angry expression from the effort of trying to overcome his shyness.
"What are the Shtcherbatskys up to? Same as ever?" he said.
Stepan Arkadyevitch, who had long known that Levin was in love with his sister-in-law Kitty, gave the faintest of smiles, his eyes sparkling.
"You said a few words, but I can't answer in a few words, because... Excuse me a minute..."

A secretary came in, with the respectful familiarity and the modest awareness, typical of every secretary, of knowing the business better than his chief; he went up to Oblonsky with some papers and began, under the pretext of asking a question, to put forward an objection. Stepan Arkadyevitch, without hearing him out, laid his hand warmly on the secretary's sleeve.

"No, do as I told you," he said, softening his words with a smile, and after a brief explanation of how he saw the matter, he turned away from the papers and said, "Do it that way, please, Zahar Nikititch."

The secretary retreated in confusion. During the exchange with the secretary, Levin had completely recovered from his embarrassment. He was standing with his elbows on the back of a chair, an ironical attentiveness on his face.
"I don't get it, I don't get it," he said.
"What don't you get?" said Oblonsky, smiling as brightly as before and picking up a cigarette. He was expecting some odd outburst from Levin.
"I don't understand what you're doing," Levin said, shrugging. "How can you take it seriously?"
"Why not?"
"Because there's nothing to it."
"You think so, but we're overwhelmed with work."
"On paper. But there, you have a gift for it," Levin added.
"Meaning, you think there's something missing in me?"

"Perhaps," said Levin. "But all the same, I admire your grandeur and am proud to have a friend who's such an important person. You haven't answered my question, though," he went on, making a desperate effort to look Oblonsky in the face.

"Oh, all right. You wait a bit and you'll come to it yourself. It's all very well for you, with your six thousand acres in the Karazinsky district, and muscles like that, and the freshness of a girl of twelve; but you'll be one of us yet. As for your question — there's no change, but it's a pity you've been away so long."
"Oh, why?" Levin asked, panic-stricken.
"Oh, nothing," Oblonsky answered. "We'll talk about it. But what brought you up to town?"
"Oh, we'll talk about that too, later on," Levin said, blushing again up to his ears.

"All right. I see," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "I'd ask you to come to us, you know, but my wife's not feeling quite herself. But I'll tell you what: if you want to see them, they'll be at the Zoological Gardens from four to five today. Kitty is skating. Drive over there, and I'll come fetch you, and we'll go and dine somewhere together."
"Excellent. Good-bye till then, then."
"Now mind, you'll forget, I know you — or you'll run off home to the country!" Stepan Arkadyevitch called out, laughing.
"No, I really won't!"
And Levin walked out of the room, only remembering when he was already in the doorway that he had forgotten to say goodbye to Oblonsky's colleagues.
"That gentleman must be a man of great energy," said Grinevitch, after Levin had gone.

"Yes, my dear boy," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, nodding. "He's a lucky fellow. Over six thousand acres in the Karazinsky district, everything ahead of him, and what youth and vigor! Not like some of us."
"You have a great deal to complain of, don't you, Stepan Arkadyevitch?"
"Ah yes, I'm in a poor way, a bad way," Stepan Arkadyevitch said with a heavy sigh.

title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: When Oblonsky asked Levin what had brought him to town, Levin blushed, and was furious with himself for blushing, because he could not answer, "I've come to propose to your sister-in-law," though that was exactly why he had come.

The Levin and Shtcherbatsky families were old, noble Moscow families and had always been on close, friendly terms. The friendship had grown still closer during Levin's student years. He had prepared for the university alongside the young Prince Shtcherbatsky, brother of Kitty and Dolly, and they had entered together. In those days Levin was often in the Shtcherbatskys' house, and he was in love with the Shtcherbatsky household. Strange as it may sound, it was the household, the family, that Konstantin Levin was in love with, especially the female half of it. Levin did not remember his own mother, and his only sister was older than he was, so it was in the Shtcherbatskys' house that he first saw the inner life of an old, noble, cultivated, and honorable family — the inner life he had been deprived of by his father's and mother's deaths. All the members of that family, especially the women, appeared to him wrapped in some kind of mysterious, poetic veil, and he not only saw no faults in them at all, but assumed that under the poetic veil that hid them there had to be the loftiest sentiments and every possible perfection. Why it was that the three young ladies had to speak French one day and English the next; why at certain hours they took turns playing the piano, whose sounds rose into their brother's room above where the students were working; why they were visited by those professors of French literature, of music, of drawing, of dancing; why at certain hours all three young ladies, with Mademoiselle Linon, drove in the carriage to the Tversky boulevard, dressed in their satin cloaks — Dolly in a long one, Natalia in a half-length one, and Kitty in one so short that her shapely legs in tight red stockings were visible to everyone; why they had to walk along the Tversky boulevard escorted by a footman with a gold cockade in his hat — all of this, and much more that was done in their mysterious world, he did not understand, but he was sure that everything done there was very good, and he was in love with precisely the mystery of it all.

In his student days he had almost been in love with the eldest, Dolly, but she had soon married Oblonsky. Then he had started being in love with the second sister. He felt vaguely that he was obliged to be in love with one of the sisters, only he could not quite work out which. But Natalia, too, had hardly come out into society before she married the diplomat Lvov. Kitty had still been a child when Levin left the university. The young Shtcherbatsky had gone into the navy, drowned in the Baltic, and Levin's contact with the Shtcherbatskys, in spite of his friendship with Oblonsky, became less close. But when early in the winter of that year Levin came to Moscow, after a year in the country, and saw the Shtcherbatskys again, he realized which of the three sisters he was truly meant to love.

You would think nothing could be simpler than for him, a man of good family, rather rich than poor, and thirty-two years old, to make young Princess Shtcherbatskaya an offer of marriage; in all likelihood he would have been seen at once as a good match. But Levin was in love, and so it seemed to him that Kitty was so perfect in every way that she was a creature far above anything of this earth, and that he was a creature so low and so earthly that it could not even be imagined that other people, or she herself, could regard him as worthy of her.

After spending two months in Moscow in a kind of trance, seeing Kitty almost every day at the social events he attended just to see her, he abruptly decided that it could not be, and went back to the country.

Levin's conviction that it could not be was founded on the idea that in her family's eyes he was an undesirable, worthless match for the charming Kitty, and that Kitty herself could not love him. In her family's eyes he had no ordinary, well-defined career or social position, while by this time his contemporaries, when he was thirty-two, were already, one a colonel, another a professor, another a director of a bank and railways, or president of a board like Oblonsky. But he (he knew very well how he must look to others) was a country gentleman, occupied with breeding cattle, shooting game, and putting up barns — in other words, a man of no special ability who had not made anything of himself, and who was doing exactly what, in the eyes of the world, people fit for nothing else do.

The mysterious, enchanting Kitty herself, surely, could not love such an ugly man as he believed himself to be, and, above all, such an ordinary, in no way striking man. On top of that, his attitude toward Kitty in the past — the attitude of a grown man to a child, arising from his friendship with her brother — seemed to him another obstacle to love. An ugly, good-natured man like himself, he supposed, might be liked as a friend; but to be loved with the kind of love he felt for Kitty, you had to be a handsome man, and, above all, a distinguished one.

He had been told that women often went for ugly, ordinary men, but he didn't believe it; he was judging by himself, and for his part he could never have fallen for anyone but a beautiful, mysterious, exceptional woman.

But after two months alone in the country, he was convinced that this was not one of those passions he had known in his early youth, that this feeling gave him not a moment's rest, that he could not live without settling the question of whether or not she would be his wife, and that his despair had come only from his own imaginings — that he had no real proof he would be rejected. And so he had come to Moscow with the firm intention of making an offer, and, if accepted, getting married. Or... he could not begin to imagine what would become of him if he was refused.

title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Arriving in Moscow by a morning train, Levin had put up at the house of his elder half-brother Koznishev. After changing his clothes he went down to his brother's study, intending to talk to him at once about the reason for his visit and to ask his advice; but his brother was not alone. A well-known professor of philosophy was with him, who had come from Harkov expressly to clear up a disagreement that had arisen between them on a very important philosophical question. The professor was conducting a heated crusade against materialists. Sergey Koznishev had been following this crusade with interest, and after reading the professor's most recent article he had written to him stating his objections. He had accused the professor of conceding too much to the materialists. And the professor had promptly turned up to argue the matter out. The point under discussion was the question then in fashion: is there a line to be drawn between psychological and physiological phenomena in man, and if so, where?
Sergey Ivanovitch greeted his brother with the cool, friendly smile he had for everyone, and after introducing him to the professor, went on with the conversation.

A small man in spectacles, with a narrow forehead, tore himself away from the discussion for a second to greet Levin, and then went on talking without paying any further attention to him. Levin sat down to wait for the professor to leave, but soon got interested in the subject under discussion.

Levin had come across the magazine articles the two of them were arguing about, and had read them, finding them interesting as an extension of the basic principles of science, which were familiar to him from his university days as a natural-science student. But he had never connected these scientific conclusions — about the origin of man as an animal, about reflex action, biology, and sociology — with the questions about the meaning of life and death that had lately been more and more on his mind.

As he listened to his brother's argument with the professor, he noticed that they were connecting these scientific questions to those spiritual ones, that at times they almost touched on the latter; but every time they were close to what seemed to him the central point, they promptly retreated and plunged again into a sea of fine distinctions, qualifications, quotations, allusions, and appeals to authority, and he had a hard time following what they were even saying.

"I cannot allow it," said Sergey Ivanovitch with his usual clarity, precision of expression, and elegance of phrase. "I cannot in any case agree with Keiss that my entire conception of the external world has been derived from perceptions. The most fundamental idea, the idea of existence, has not been transmitted to me through sensation; there is, in fact, no special sense-organ to transmit such an idea."

"Yes, but Wurt and Knaust and Pripasov would answer that your consciousness of existence is derived from the combination of all your sensations — that this consciousness of existence is the result of your sensations. Wurt, in fact, says plainly that, granted there are no sensations, it follows that there is no idea of existence."
"I would maintain the opposite," began Sergey Ivanovitch.
But here it seemed to Levin that just as they were on the verge of the real point, they were retreating again, and he made up his mind to put a question to the professor.
"By that reasoning, if my senses are destroyed, if my body is dead, I can have no existence of any kind?" he asked.

The professor, irritated, and as if in real mental pain at the interruption, looked around at the odd questioner, who looked more like a bargeman than a philosopher, and turned his eyes to Sergey Ivanovitch, as if to ask: what is one supposed to say to a man like this? But Sergey Ivanovitch, who had been arguing with far less heat and far less one-sidedness than the professor, and who had enough breadth of mind both to answer the professor and to grasp the simple, natural angle the question had been put from, smiled and said:
"That question we have no right to answer yet."

"We don't have the necessary data," the professor chimed in, and went back to his argument. "No," he said; "I would point out the fact that if, as Pripasov directly claims, perception is based on sensation, then we are bound to distinguish sharply between these two concepts."
Levin listened no more, and just waited for the professor to leave.

title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: Once the professor had taken his leave, Sergey Ivanovitch turned to his brother.
"Glad you've come. For long? How's the farming going?"
Levin knew his elder brother had little interest in farming and was only asking out of consideration for him, so he only told him about the sale of his wheat and about money matters.

Levin had meant to tell his brother of his determination to get married and to ask his advice; he had in fact firmly resolved to do so. But after seeing his brother, after listening to his conversation with the professor, after hearing the unconsciously patronizing tone in which his brother questioned him about agricultural matters (their mother's estate had not been divided, and Levin was managing both their shares), Levin felt that for some reason he could not bring himself to begin talking about his intention to marry. He felt his brother would not look at it the way he himself wished he would.
"Well, how is your district council doing?" asked Sergey Ivanovitch, who was very interested in these local boards and attached great importance to them.
"I really don't know."
"What? But you're surely a member of the board?"
"No, I'm not a member anymore; I've resigned," Levin answered, "and I don't go to the meetings anymore."
"What a pity," Sergey Ivanovitch said, frowning.
In self-defense, Levin began to describe what went on at the meetings in his district.

"That's how it always is!" Sergey Ivanovitch cut in. "We Russians are always like this. Maybe it's our strong point, really, this knack for seeing our own shortcomings; but we overdo it, we comfort ourselves with the irony we always have ready on the tip of our tongues. All I'm saying is, give the rights of our local self-government to any other European people — why, the Germans or the English would have worked their way to liberty through them, while we simply turn them into a joke."
"But what can one do?" said Levin penitently. "It was my last effort. And I really did try with all my soul. I can't. I'm just no good at it."
"It's not that you're no good at it," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "It's that you don't look at it the way you should."
"Perhaps not," Levin answered dejectedly.
"Oh — do you know our brother Nikolay has turned up again?"

This brother Nikolay was the elder brother of Konstantin Levin and the half-brother of Sergey Ivanovitch: a man utterly ruined, who had run through most of his fortune, was living in the strangest and lowest company, and had quarreled with both his brothers.
"What did you say?" Levin cried in horror. "How do you know?"
"Prokofy saw him in the street."
"Here in Moscow? Where is he? Do you know?" Levin got up from his chair as if he were on the point of going to find him at once.

"I'm sorry I told you," said Sergey Ivanovitch, shaking his head at his younger brother's agitation. "I sent to find out where he is living, and sent him his IOU to Trubin, which I paid. This is what he sent back to me."
And Sergey Ivanovitch took a note out from under a paperweight and handed it to his brother.
Levin read, in the strange but familiar handwriting: "I humbly beg you to leave me alone. That's the only favor I ask of my gracious brothers. — Nikolay Levin."
Levin read it, and without raising his head stood with the note in his hands across from Sergey Ivanovitch.
There was a struggle inside him between the wish to put his unhappy brother out of his mind for the moment and the awareness that it would be base to do so.
"He obviously wants to insult me," Sergey Ivanovitch went on; "but he can't insult me, and I would have wished with all my heart to help him, but I know it's impossible to do."
"Yes, yes," Levin repeated. "I understand and respect your position toward him; but I'm going to go see him."

"If you want to, then do; but I wouldn't advise it," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "As far as I'm concerned, I have no fear of your doing it; he won't set you against me. But for your own sake, I'd say you'd do better not to go. You can't do him any good; still, do as you like."
"Most likely I can't do any good — but I feel, especially at a moment like this... but that's another matter — I feel I couldn't be at peace."

"Well, that I don't understand," said Sergey Ivanovitch. "One thing I do understand," he added; "it's a lesson in humility. I've come to look very differently and more charitably on what is called shameful since brother Nikolay became what he is... you know what he did."
"Oh, it's awful, awful!" Levin repeated.

After getting his brother's address from Sergey Ivanovitch's footman, Levin was on the point of going to see him at once, but on second thought he decided to put the visit off until evening. The first thing to do, to set his heart at ease, was to finish what he had come to Moscow to do. From his brother's, Levin went to Oblonsky's office, and after getting news of the Shtcherbatskys from him, he drove off to the place where he had been told he might find Kitty.

title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: At four o'clock, his heart pounding, Levin stepped out of a hired sledge at the Zoological Gardens and turned along the path toward the frozen mounds and the skating ground, knowing he would certainly find her there, since he had seen the Shtcherbatskys' carriage at the entrance.

It was a bright, frosty day. Rows of carriages, sledges, drivers, and policemen stood along the approach. Crowds of well-dressed people, their hats bright in the sunlight, swarmed about the entrance and along the carefully swept paths between the little houses decorated in the carved Russian style. The old curly birches of the gardens, every twig laden with snow, looked as if they had been freshly dressed in sacred vestments.

He walked along the path toward the skating ground, repeating to himself, "You mustn't get excited. You have to be calm. What's the matter with you? What do you want? Be quiet, stupid," he ordered his heart. And the more he tried to compose himself, the more breathless he found himself. An acquaintance met him and called him by his name, but Levin did not even recognize him. He went on toward the mounds, from which came the clank of the chains of sledges as they were dragged up or slid down, the rumble of the sliding sledges, and the sound of cheerful voices. He walked on a few steps, and the skating ground lay open before him, and at once, among all the skaters, he knew her.

He knew she was there by the joy and the terror that gripped his heart. She was standing at the far end of the ground, talking to a lady. There was apparently nothing striking about either her dress or her posture. But for Levin she was as easy to spot in that crowd as a rose among nettles. Everything was made bright by her. She was the smile that lit up everything around her. "Can I really go out there onto the ice, go up to her?" he thought. The spot where she stood seemed to him a holy place, untouchable, and there was a moment when he nearly turned back, so overwhelmed he was with terror. He had to make an effort to master himself, to remind himself that all kinds of people were moving about near her and that he too might come there to skate. He walked down, avoiding looking at her for a long time as one avoids looking at the sun, yet seeing her, as one sees the sun, without looking.

On that day of the week and at that hour, people of one set, all of them acquainted with each other, used to gather on the ice. There were expert skaters showing off their skill, beginners clinging to chairs with timid, awkward movements, boys, and elderly people skating for the sake of their health. They seemed to Levin a select company of blessed beings, because they were here, near her. All the skaters, it seemed, with perfect self-possession, skated toward her, skated past her, even spoke to her, and were happy, quite apart from her, enjoying the excellent ice and the fine weather.
Kitty's cousin Nikolay Shtcherbatsky, wearing a short jacket and tight trousers, was sitting on a garden bench with his skates already on. When he spotted Levin, he called out:
"Ah, the best skater in Russia! Been here long? First-rate ice — put your skates on."

"I haven't got my skates," Levin answered, amazed at this boldness and ease in her presence, and not losing sight of her for a second, though he was not looking at her. He felt as though the sun were coming close to him. She was in a corner, and turning her slender feet outwards in their high boots with obvious timidity, she was skating toward him. A boy in Russian dress, desperately swinging his arms and bent almost to the ground, came up alongside her. She skated a little uncertainly; taking her hands out of the little muff that hung from a cord, she held them ready in case of need, and, looking toward Levin, whom she had recognized, smiled at him and at her own fears. When she had got around the turn, she pushed off with one foot and skated straight up to Shtcherbatsky. Grabbing his arm, she nodded smiling to Levin. She was more wonderful than he had imagined her.

When he thought of her, he could call up a vivid picture of her, especially the charm of that little fair head set so freely on her shapely girlish shoulders, so full of childlike brightness and good humor. The childlikeness of her expression, together with the delicate beauty of her figure, made up her special charm, and he fully understood that. But what always struck him about her as unexpected was the expression of her eyes — soft, serene, and truthful — and, above all, her smile, which always transported Levin into an enchanted world where he felt himself softened and tender, as he remembered being on certain days in his early childhood.
"Have you been here long?" she said, holding out her hand to him. "Thank you," she added, when he picked up the handkerchief that had slipped out of her muff.

"I? Not long... yesterday... I mean today... I arrived," Levin answered, too rattled to take in her question at once. "I was meaning to come and see you," he said; and then, remembering with what intention he was looking for her, he was at once overcome with confusion and blushed.
"I didn't know you could skate, and skate so well."
She looked at him seriously, as if trying to make out the cause of his confusion.
"Your praise means a lot. The tradition lives on here that you're the best of the skaters," she said, brushing a fleck of frost off her muff with her little black-gloved hand.
"Yes, I used to skate with a passion; I wanted to reach perfection."
"You do everything with passion, I think," she said, smiling. "I'd love to see how you skate. Put on some skates and let's skate together."
"Skate together! Can that really be?" thought Levin, gazing at her.
"I'll put them on right away," he said.
And he went off to get skates.

"It's been a long time since we've seen you here, sir," said the attendant, supporting his foot and tightening the heel of the skate. "Apart from you, there's not one of the gentlemen who's a first-rate skater. Is that right?" he said, tightening the strap.

"Oh, yes, yes; hurry, please," Levin answered, barely able to hold back the smile of rapture that kept spreading over his face. "Yes," he thought, "this — this is life, this is happiness! _Together,_ she said; _let us skate together!_ Speak to her now? But that's exactly why I'm afraid to speak — because I'm happy now, happy at least in hope... And then? But I must! I must! I must! Away with weakness!"

Levin got to his feet, took off his overcoat, and scurrying over the rough ice around the hut, came out onto the smooth ice and skated effortlessly, as if by mere force of will, speeding up and slowing down and changing course. He approached her timidly, but again her smile reassured him.
She put her hand in his, and the two of them set off side by side, picking up speed, and the faster they went the tighter she gripped him.
"With you I'd learn quickly; I somehow feel I can trust you," she said to him.

"And I trust myself when you're leaning on me," he said, and was at once panicked at what he had said, and blushed. And in fact, no sooner had he spoken than her face, as if the sun had gone behind a cloud, lost all its friendliness, and Levin caught the familiar change in her expression that meant her thoughts were at work; a crease appeared on her smooth brow.
"Is something troubling you? — though I have no right to ask such a question," he added hurriedly.
"Oh, why so?... No, there's nothing troubling me," she answered coldly; and added at once, "You haven't seen Mlle. Linon yet?"
"Not yet."
"Go and speak to her; she likes you so much."

"What's wrong? I've offended her. Lord help me!" Levin thought, and flew over to the old Frenchwoman with the gray ringlets, who was sitting on a bench. Smiling and showing her false teeth, she greeted him as an old friend.

"Yes, you see, we're growing up," she said to him, glancing toward Kitty, "and growing old. _Tiny bear_ is big now!" the Frenchwoman went on, laughing, and reminded him of the joke he had made about the three young ladies whom he had compared to the three bears in the English nursery tale. "Do you remember? That's what you used to call them."
He had no memory of it whatsoever, but she had been laughing at the joke for ten years now and was attached to it.
"Now go and skate, go and skate. Our Kitty has learned to skate beautifully, hasn't she?"

When Levin darted up to Kitty her face was no longer stern; her eyes looked at him with the same sincerity and friendliness, but Levin sensed in that friendliness a certain deliberate composure. And he felt depressed. After a little talk about her old governess and her quirks, she asked him about his life.
"Surely you must be dull in the country in the winter, aren't you?" she said.

"No, I'm not dull, I'm very busy," he said, feeling that she was holding him in check with her composed tone, which he wouldn't have the strength to break through, just as had happened at the beginning of the winter.
"Will you be in town long?" Kitty asked him.

"I don't know," he answered, not paying attention to what he was saying. The thought that if he let her quiet, friendly tone hold him in check he would end up going back without deciding anything came into his head, and he resolved to fight it.
"How can you not know?"
"I don't know. It depends on you," he said, and was instantly horrified at his own words.

Whether it was because she had heard what he said, or because she did not want to hear it, she made a kind of stumble, struck out twice with her foot, and skated hurriedly away from him. She skated up to Mlle. Linon, said something to her, and went toward the pavilion where the ladies took off their skates.
"My God! What have I done? Merciful God, help me, guide me," Levin prayed silently — and at the same time, needing some violent exertion, he cut inner and outer circles across the ice.

At that moment one of the young men, the best of the day's skaters, came out of the coffee-house in his skates, a cigarette in his mouth. Taking a run, he hurled himself down the steps in his skates, clattering and bouncing. He flew down, and, without even shifting the position of his hands, skated away over the ice.
"Ah, that's a new trick!" said Levin, and promptly ran up to the top to try this new trick himself.
"Don't break your neck — it takes practice!" Nikolay Shtcherbatsky shouted after him.

Levin went to the steps, took as good a run as he could from the top, and dashed down, balancing in this unfamiliar move with his hands. On the last step he stumbled, but barely touching the ice with his hand, with a violent effort recovered himself, and skated off, laughing.

"How splendid, how nice he is!" Kitty was thinking just then, as she came out of the pavilion with Mlle. Linon, and looked toward him with a smile of quiet affection, as if he were a favorite brother. "And can it be my fault? Could I have done anything wrong? They talk of flirtation. I know it's not him I love; but still I'm happy with him, and he's so jolly. Only — why did he say that?..." she mused.

Seeing Kitty going away, and her mother meeting her at the steps, Levin, flushed from his hard exercise, stood still and thought for a moment. Then he took off his skates and caught up with mother and daughter at the entrance to the gardens.
"Delighted to see you," said Princess Shtcherbatskaya. "On Thursdays we're at home, as always."
"Today, then?"
"We shall be pleased to see you," the princess said stiffly.
Her mother's stiffness wounded Kitty, and she couldn't help trying to soften the coldness. She turned her head and said, smiling:
"Good-bye till this evening."

Just then Stepan Arkadyevitch, his hat cocked to one side, his face and eyes beaming, strode into the gardens like a conquering hero. But as he came up to his mother-in-law, his tone, when she asked after Dolly, was mournful and crestfallen. After a brief, subdued and dejected exchange with her, he threw out his chest again and slipped his arm into Levin's.
"Well, shall we go?" he asked. "I've been thinking about you all this time, and I'm very, very glad you've come," he said, looking at him meaningfully.
"Yes, come on," answered Levin in ecstasy, hearing over and over the sound of that voice saying, "Good-bye till this evening," and seeing the smile that had come with it.
"To the England, or the Hermitage?"
"I don't mind which."

"All right then, the England," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, choosing that restaurant because he owed more there than at the Hermitage, and so considered it a kind of meanness to avoid it. "Have you got a sledge? Good — I sent my carriage home."

The friends hardly spoke the whole way. Levin was wondering what that change in Kitty's expression had meant, telling himself by turns that there was hope, then sinking into despair, seeing clearly that his hopes were mad — and yet all the while he felt himself to be quite another man, utterly unlike what he had been before her smile and those words, "Good-bye till this evening."
Throughout the drive, Stepan Arkadyevitch was lost in putting together the menu for dinner.
"You like turbot, don't you?" he said to Levin as they were arriving.
"Eh?" Levin answered. "Turbot? Yes, I'm _awfully_ fond of turbot."

title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: When Levin went into the restaurant with Oblonsky, he could not help noticing a certain quality of expression — a kind of contained radiance — about Stepan Arkadyevitch's face and his whole figure. Oblonsky took off his overcoat, and with his hat over one ear walked into the dining-room, giving orders to the Tatar waiters who were clustered around him in evening coats with napkins on their arms. Bowing to right and left to the people he met, and here, as everywhere, greeting acquaintances joyfully, he went up to the sideboard for a preliminary appetizer of fish and vodka, and said something to the painted Frenchwoman behind the counter, all ribbons, lace, and ringlets, so amusing that even she was moved to genuine laughter. Levin for his part avoided taking any vodka simply because he felt such a loathing of that Frenchwoman, who seemed to be made up entirely of false hair, _poudre de riz,_ and _vinaigre de toilette_. He hurried to move away from her, as from a dirty place. His whole soul was filled with memories of Kitty, and there was a smile of triumph and happiness shining in his eyes.

"This way, your excellency, please. Your excellency won't be disturbed here," said a particularly persistent, white-headed old Tatar with huge hips and coat-tails gaping wide behind him. "Walk in, your excellency," he said to Levin too, by way of showing his respect for Stepan Arkadyevitch and being attentive to his guest as well.

Instantly flinging a fresh cloth over the round table under the bronze chandelier, even though there was already a cloth on it, he pushed up velvet chairs and stood before Stepan Arkadyevitch with a napkin and a menu in his hands, waiting for orders.
"If you'd prefer it, your excellency, a private room will be free in a moment; Prince Golistin and a lady. Fresh oysters have come in."
"Ah! Oysters."
Stepan Arkadyevitch became thoughtful.
"What if we changed our plan, Levin?" he said, keeping his finger on the menu. And his face wore a look of serious hesitation. "Are the oysters good? Mind, now."
"They're Flensburg, your excellency. We've no Ostend."
"Flensburg will do, but are they fresh?"
"Only came in yesterday."
"Well then, what if we were to start with oysters, and so change the whole plan? Eh?"
