"It's all the same to me. What I'd really like is cabbage soup and porridge, but there's of course nothing like that here."
"_Porridge à la Russe,_ your honor would like?" said the Tatar, bending down to Levin as if a nurse speaking to a child.

"No, joking aside, whatever you order will be good. I've been skating, and I'm hungry. And don't imagine," he added, catching a look of dissatisfaction on Oblonsky's face, "that I won't appreciate your choice. I'm fond of good things."

"I should hope so! After all, it's one of the pleasures of life," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "All right, then, my friend, bring us two dozen oysters — better make it three — clear soup with vegetables..."
"_Printanière,_" prompted the Tatar. But Stepan Arkadyevitch evidently did not care to allow him the pleasure of giving the dishes their French names.
"With vegetables in it, you understand. After that, turbot in a heavy sauce; then... roast beef — and make sure it's good. Yes, perhaps capons too, and then dessert."

The Tatar, remembering that it was Stepan Arkadyevitch's way not to call the dishes by their French names on the menu, did not repeat them after him, but could not resist running through the whole menu to himself according to the card: "_Soupe printanière, turbot, sauce Beaumarchais, poulard à l'estragon, macédoine de fruits,_" and so on; and then instantly, as though worked by springs, he laid down one bound menu and picked up another, the wine list, and held it out to Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"What shall we drink?"
"What you like, only not too much. Champagne," said Levin.
"What — to start with? You're right, though, I dare say. Do you like the white seal?"
"_Cachet blanc,_" prompted the Tatar.
"Very well, then, give us that brand with the oysters, and then we'll see."
"Yes, sir. And what table wine?"
"You can give us Nuits. Oh, no, better the classic Chablis."
"Yes, sir. And _your_ cheese, your excellency?"
"Oh, yes, Parmesan. Or would you prefer another?"
"No, it's all the same to me," said Levin, unable to keep back a smile.
The Tatar shot off, coat-tails flying, and five minutes later swept back in carrying a platter of opened oysters on their mother-of-pearl shells, with a bottle wedged between his fingers.
Stepan Arkadyevitch crushed the starched napkin, tucked it into his waistcoat, settled his arms comfortably, and got to work on the oysters.

"Not bad," he said, prying the oysters off their pearly shells with a silver fork and swallowing them one after another. "Not bad," he repeated, lifting his dewy, sparkling eyes from Levin to the Tatar.

Levin ate the oysters too, though white bread and cheese would have suited him better. But he was admiring Oblonsky. Even the Tatar, uncorking the bottle and pouring the sparkling wine into the delicate glasses, glanced at Stepan Arkadyevitch and adjusted his white cravat with a visible smile of satisfaction.
"You don't really care for oysters, do you?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, draining his wine-glass. "Or are you worried about something? Eh?"

He wanted Levin to be in good spirits. It wasn't that Levin was out of spirits; he was ill at ease. With what was in his soul, he felt sore and uncomfortable in the restaurant, surrounded by private rooms where men were dining with women, in all the fuss and bustle; the bronzes, looking-glasses, gaslight, and waiters — all of it offended him. He was afraid of soiling what his soul was brimming with.
"Me? Yes, I am; but also, all this bothers me," he said. "You can't imagine how strange it all looks to a country person like me — as strange as that gentleman's nails I saw at your office..."
"Yes, I saw how interested you were in poor Grinevitch's nails," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, laughing.

"It's too much for me," Levin answered. "Try, will you, to put yourself in my place, take the country man's point of view. We in the country try to keep our hands in such a state as will be most convenient for working. So we cut our nails; sometimes we roll up our sleeves. And here people deliberately let their nails grow as long as they will, and link on saucer-sized cuff-studs, so that they can't do a thing with their hands."
Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled brightly.
"Oh yes, it's just a sign that he has no need to do rough work. His work is with the mind..."

"Maybe. But still it's strange to me, just as at this moment it seems strange to me that we country folks try to get our meals down as fast as we can, so as to be ready for our work, while here we're trying to draw our meal out as long as possible, and to that end eating oysters..."
"Of course," Stepan Arkadyevitch objected. "But that's just the aim of civilization — to make everything into a pleasure."
"Well, if that's the aim, I'd rather be a savage."
"And so you are a savage. All you Levins are savages."
Levin sighed. The thought of his brother Nikolay came back to him; he felt ashamed and sore, and frowned — but Oblonsky launched into a subject that immediately caught his attention.
"Oh, are you going tonight to our people, the Shtcherbatskys, I mean?" he said, his eyes sparkling meaningfully as he pushed aside the empty oyster shells and pulled the cheese toward him.
"Yes, I'll certainly go," Levin replied; "though I had the impression the princess wasn't very warm in her invitation."

"Nonsense! That's just her manner... Come on, boy, the soup!... That's her manner — _grande dame,_" said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "I'm coming too, but I have to drop in on Countess Bonina's rehearsal. Come, isn't it true that you're a savage? How do you explain the abrupt way you vanished from Moscow? The Shtcherbatskys were forever asking me about you, as if I were supposed to know. The only thing I know is that you always do what no one else does."
"Yes," said Levin, slowly and with feeling, "you're right. I am a savage. Only my savageness isn't in having gone away; it's in coming back now. Now I have come..."
"Oh, what a lucky fellow you are!" broke in Stepan Arkadyevitch, looking into Levin's eyes.
"Why?"
"'I know a gallant steed by tokens sure,
And by his eyes I know a youth in love,'"
declaimed Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Everything lies ahead of you."
"Why, is it over for you already?"
"No; not over exactly, but the future is yours, and the present is mine, and the present — well, it's not all it might be."
"How so?"

"Oh, things go wrong. But I don't want to talk about myself, and besides, I can't explain it all," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Well — why have you come to Moscow, then?... Hi, take this away!" he called to the Tatar.
"You guess?" answered Levin, his eyes like deep wells of light fixed on Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"I guess, but I can't be the first to bring it up. You can tell from that whether I guess right or wrong," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, looking at Levin with a subtle smile.
"Well — and what do you have to say to me?" said Levin in a trembling voice, feeling that every muscle in his face was trembling too. "How do you look at the question?"
Stepan Arkadyevitch slowly drained his glass of Chablis, never taking his eyes off Levin.
"Me?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "There's nothing I want more — nothing! It would be the best thing that could be."
"But you're not making a mistake? You do know what we're talking about?" said Levin, piercing him with his eyes. "You think it's possible?"
"I think it's possible. Why shouldn't it be?"
"No! Do you really think it's possible? No, tell me everything you think! Oh, but if... if I'm to be refused!... I really feel sure of it..."
"Why should you think that?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling at his agitation.
"It seems so to me sometimes. That would be awful for me, and for her too."
"Oh well, in any case there's nothing awful about it for a girl. Every girl's proud of an offer."
"Yes, every girl — but not her."

Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled. He knew that feeling of Levin's so well — that for him all the girls in the world were divided into two classes: one class, all the girls in the world except her, and those girls with all kinds of human weaknesses, very ordinary girls; the other class, she alone, with no weaknesses of any sort and higher than all humanity.
"Wait, take some sauce," he said, holding back Levin's hand as it pushed away the sauce.
Levin obediently helped himself to some sauce, but would not let Stepan Arkadyevitch go on with his dinner.

"No, wait, wait," he said. "You have to understand, this is a matter of life and death for me. I've never spoken to anyone about this. And there's no one I could speak about it to, except you. You know we're utterly unlike each other — different tastes and views and everything; but I know you're fond of me, and you understand me, and that's why I like you so much. But for God's sake, be completely straight with me."

"I'm telling you what I think," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling. "But I'll say more: my wife is a remarkable woman..." Stepan Arkadyevitch sighed, remembering his position with his wife, and after a moment's silence went on, "She has the gift of seeing things in advance. She sees right through people; but that's not all — she knows what's going to happen, especially when it comes to marriages. She foretold, for instance, that Princess Shahovskaya would marry Brenteln. No one would believe it, but it came to pass. And she's on your side."
"How do you mean?"
"It's not just that she likes you — she says Kitty is certain to be your wife."
At these words Levin's face suddenly lit up with a smile, a smile not far from tears of emotion.
"She actually says that?" Levin cried. "I've always said your wife is exquisite. There, that's enough — enough said about it now," he added, getting up from his chair.
"All right, but do sit down."
But Levin could not sit down. He paced the cramped little room twice with his firm step, blinking hard so his tears wouldn't spill over, and only then took his seat at the table.

"You must understand," he said, "this isn't love. I've been in love, but it's not that. It's not my feeling, but some kind of force outside me that has taken hold of me. I went away, you see, because I had decided it could never be, you understand, like a happiness that doesn't exist on earth; but I've struggled with myself, and I see there's no living without it. And it has to be settled."
"Why did you go away?"

"Oh, hold on a minute! Ah, the thoughts that come crowding in! The questions you have to ask yourself! Listen. You can't imagine what you've done for me with what you said. I'm so happy that I've become positively hateful; I've forgotten everything. I heard today that my brother Nikolay... you know, he's here... I'd even forgotten him. It seems to me that he's happy too. It's a kind of madness. But there's one thing that's awful... Now, you've been married, you know the feeling... it's awful that we — old — with a past... not of love, but of sins... are brought suddenly so close to a pure, innocent creature; it's loathsome, and that's why one can't help feeling oneself unworthy."
"Oh well, you haven't many sins on your conscience."
"Alas — all the same," Levin said, "when with loathing I go back over my life, I shudder and curse and bitterly regret it... Yes."
"What would you have? The world is made so," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"My one comfort is that prayer I've always loved: 'Forgive me not according to my unworthiness, but according to Thy loving-kindness.' That is the only way she can forgive me."

title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: Levin drained his glass, and they were silent for a while.
"There's one other thing I should mention. Do you know Vronsky?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked Levin.
"No, I don't. Why do you ask?"
"Give us another bottle," Stepan Arkadyevitch ordered the Tatar, who was refilling their glasses and fussing around them just when he wasn't wanted.
"Why you ought to know Vronsky is that he's one of your rivals."
"Who's Vronsky?" said Levin, and his face was transformed in an instant from the look of childlike rapture Oblonsky had just been admiring into something angry and ugly.

"Vronsky is one of the sons of Count Kirill Ivanovitch Vronsky and one of the finest specimens of Petersburg's gilded youth. I met him in Tver when I was there on official business and he came down for the recruit levy. Tremendously rich, handsome, well-connected, an aide-de-camp, and on top of all that a very nice, good-natured fellow. But he's more than just a good-natured fellow, as I've discovered here — he's a cultivated man, too, and very intelligent; he's a man who will make his mark."
Levin scowled and said nothing.
"Well, he turned up here soon after you'd left, and from what I can see he's head over heels in love with Kitty, and you know that her mother..."
"Excuse me, but I know nothing of all that," Levin said, frowning darkly. And immediately he remembered his brother Nikolay, and how hateful it was that he had been able to forget him.

"Wait, wait a moment," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling and touching his hand. "I've told you what I know, and I'll say it again: in this delicate and tender matter, as far as one can guess, I believe the chances are in your favor."
Levin dropped back into his chair; his face was pale.
"But I would advise you to settle the thing as soon as you can," Oblonsky went on, filling up his glass.
"No, thanks, I can't drink any more," Levin said, pushing his glass away. "I'll be drunk... Come, tell me — how are you doing?" he went on, obviously eager to change the subject.

"One more word: whatever happens, I advise you to settle the question soon. Tonight I wouldn't advise you to speak," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Go round tomorrow morning, propose in proper form, and God bless you..."
"Oh, do you still mean to come out and shoot with me? Come next spring, will you?" said Levin.

Now his whole soul was full of remorse for having begun this conversation with Stepan Arkadyevitch. A feeling like his was profaned by talk of being rivaled by some Petersburg officer, by Stepan Arkadyevitch's speculations and counsel.
Stepan Arkadyevitch smiled. He knew what was going on in Levin's soul.

"I'll come one of these days," he said. "But women, my boy — they're the pivot everything turns on. Things are in a bad way with me, very bad. And it's all because of women. Tell me honestly, now," he went on, picking up a cigar and keeping one hand on his glass; "give me your advice."
"Advice about what?"
"I'll tell you. Suppose you're married, you love your wife, but you're fascinated by another woman..."
"Excuse me, but I'm absolutely unable to understand how... just as I can't understand how I could now, after my dinner, go straight to a baker's shop and steal a roll."
Stepan Arkadyevitch's eyes sparkled more than usual.
"Why not? A roll will sometimes smell so good you can't resist it."
"Himmlisch ist's, wenn ich bezwungen
Meine irdische Begier;
Aber doch wenn's nich gelungen
Hatt' ich auch recht hübsch Plaisir!"
As he said this, Stepan Arkadyevitch gave a subtle smile. Levin too could not help smiling.

"Yes, but joking aside," Stepan Arkadyevitch went on, "you have to understand — the woman is a sweet, gentle, loving creature, poor and lonely, who has given up everything. Now, once the thing is done, can a man really cast her off? Even if one separates from her so as not to break up family life, can one help feeling for her, helping her get on her feet, easing her lot?"

"Well, you'll have to excuse me on that score. You know that for me all women fall into two classes... at least no... it's truer to say there are women, and then there are... I've never seen exquisite fallen creatures, and I never shall; creatures like that painted Frenchwoman at the counter with her ringlets are vermin to my mind, and all fallen women are alike."
"But the Magdalen?"

"Oh, drop that. Christ would never have said those words if He had foreseen how they would be abused. Of the whole Gospel those are the only words people remember. Still, I'm not saying so much what I think as what I feel. I have a loathing for fallen women. You're afraid of spiders; I am of these vermin. Most likely you've never studied spiders and don't know their nature, and that's how it is with me."

"It's all very well for you to talk like that — it's a lot like that gentleman in Dickens who used to fling all difficult questions over his right shoulder. But denying the facts isn't an answer. What's a man to do — you tell me, what's he to do? Your wife gets older while you're still full of life. Before you've had time to look around, you find you can't love your wife with that kind of love, however much you may respect her. And then all at once love turns up, and you're done for, done for," Stepan Arkadyevitch said with weary despair.
Levin half smiled.
"Yes — you're done for," Oblonsky went on. "But what's to be done?"
"Don't steal rolls."
Stepan Arkadyevitch laughed out loud.

"Oh, moralist! But you have to understand — there are two women: one insists only on her rights, and those rights are your love, which you can't give her; and the other gives up everything for you and asks for nothing. What are you to do? How are you supposed to act? There's a fearful tragedy in it."

"If you want my profession of faith on the matter, I'll tell you that I don't believe there was any tragedy in it at all. And here's why. As I see it, love... both kinds of love, which you'll remember Plato defines in his Banquet, served as the test of men. Some men understand only one kind, and some only the other. And those who know only the non-platonic kind have no business talking about tragedy. In that sort of love there can be no tragedy whatsoever. 'Much obliged for the pleasure, my humble respects' — that's the whole tragedy. And in platonic love there can be no tragedy either, because in that love everything is clear and pure, because..."
At that instant Levin remembered his own sins and the inner struggle he had lived through. And he added, out of nowhere:
"But perhaps you're right. Very likely... I don't know, I don't know."

"Here's the thing, you see," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "You're very much all of a piece. That's your strength and your weakness. You have a character that's all of a piece, and you want the whole of life to be of a piece, too — but that's not how it is. You despise public official work because you want reality to match its purpose at every step — and that's not how it works. You want a man's work always to have a clearly defined aim, and love and family life always to be undivided — and that's not how it is either. All the variety, all the charm, all the beauty of life is made of light and shadow."
Levin sighed and made no reply. He was thinking about his own situation and not listening to Oblonsky.

And suddenly both men felt that, friends though they were and dining and drinking together as they should have done, each was thinking only of his own affairs and they had nothing to do with each other. Oblonsky had more than once felt this extreme sense of distance coming on after dinner instead of intimacy, and he knew what to do in such cases.

"Bill!" he called, and walked off into the next room, where he promptly ran into an aide-de-camp he knew and fell into conversation with him about an actress and her protector. And at once, in the conversation with the aide-de-camp, Oblonsky felt a relaxation and a relief after his exchange with Levin, which always put him under too great a mental and spiritual strain.

When the Tatar appeared with a bill for twenty-six roubles and odd kopecks, plus a tip for himself, Levin — who another time would have been horrified, like any country person, at his share of fourteen roubles — paid without noticing and set off home to dress and go on to the Shtcherbatskys', where his fate would be decided.

title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: The young Princess Kitty Shtcherbatskaya was eighteen. It was the first winter she had been out in the world. Her success in society had been greater than that of either of her older sisters, and greater even than her mother had anticipated. To say nothing of the fact that nearly all the young men dancing at the Moscow balls were in love with Kitty, two serious suitors had already presented themselves this first winter: Levin, and, right after his departure, Count Vronsky.

Levin's appearance at the beginning of the winter, his frequent visits, and his obvious love for Kitty had led to the first serious discussions between Kitty's parents about her future, and to disputes between them. The prince was on Levin's side; he said he wanted nothing better for Kitty. The princess, for her part, going around the question in the way peculiar to women, maintained that Kitty was too young, that Levin had done nothing to prove his intentions were serious, that Kitty felt no great attraction to him, and other side issues; but she did not state the main point, which was that she was looking for a better match for her daughter, and that Levin was not to her taste and she did not understand him. When Levin had abruptly left, the princess was delighted and said to her husband triumphantly, "You see, I was right." When Vronsky appeared on the scene, she was even more delighted, confirmed in her view that Kitty was going to make not merely a good match but a brilliant one.

In the mother's eyes there could be no comparison between Vronsky and Levin. She disliked Levin's strange and uncompromising opinions, and his awkwardness in society, which she put down to his pride and his queer life — as she thought of it — buried in cattle and peasants. She had not at all cared for the fact that he, who was in love with her daughter, had kept coming to the house for six weeks as though he were waiting for something, looking it over, as if afraid he might do them too great an honor by making an offer, and failing to see that a man who keeps visiting a house where there is a young unmarried girl is bound to make his intentions clear. And then suddenly, without doing so, he had disappeared. "It's just as well he isn't attractive enough for Kitty to have fallen in love with him," the mother thought.

Vronsky satisfied every one of the mother's wishes. Very wealthy, clever, of aristocratic family, on the high road to a brilliant career in the army and at court, and a fascinating man. Nothing better could be asked for.

Vronsky openly flirted with Kitty at balls, danced with her, and was constantly at the house, so there could be no doubt about how serious his intentions were. But despite this, the mother had spent the whole winter in a state of dreadful anxiety and agitation.

Princess Shtcherbatskaya herself had been married thirty years ago — an aunt of hers had arranged the match. Her husband, about whom everything was well known beforehand, had come, looked at his future bride, and been looked at himself. The matchmaking aunt had ascertained and conveyed their mutual impression. The impression had been favorable. Afterwards, on a day fixed in advance, the expected offer had been made to her parents, and accepted. Everything had gone very simply and easily. So it had seemed to the princess at least. But over her own daughters she had felt how far from simple and easy was this apparently everyday business of marrying them off. The scares she had been through, the thoughts that had been brooded over, the money that had been wasted, the arguments she had had with her husband over marrying off the two elder girls, Darya and Natalia! Now, ever since the youngest had come out, she was going through the same terrors, the same doubts, and even fiercer quarrels with her husband than she had had over the elder girls. The old prince, like all fathers, was extremely scrupulous about the honor and reputation of his daughters. He was unreasonably jealous over his daughters, especially over Kitty, who was his favorite. At every turn he had scenes with the princess for compromising her daughter. The princess had grown used to this from her older daughters, but now she felt there was more reason for the prince's touchiness. She saw that in recent years much had changed in the manners of society and that a mother's duties had grown more difficult still. She saw that girls Kitty's age formed some kind of clubs, went to some kind of lectures, mixed freely with men, drove about the streets on their own, many of them did not curtsey, and — most importantly of all — every one of them was firmly convinced that choosing her husband was her own affair, not her parents'. "Marriages aren't made nowadays the way they used to be," was thought and said by all these young girls and even by their elders. But how marriages were made now, the princess could not learn from anyone. The French fashion — parents arranging their children's future — was not accepted; it was condemned. The English fashion of complete independence for girls was also not accepted, and was impossible in Russian society. The Russian fashion of matchmaking through go-betweens was for some reason considered unseemly; it was ridiculed by everyone, including the princess herself. But how girls were to be married, and how parents were to marry them off, nobody knew. Everyone with whom the princess had discussed the matter said the same thing: "For mercy's sake, it's high time in our day to throw out all that old-fashioned business. It's the young people who have to get married, not their parents, so we ought to leave the young people to arrange things as they please." It was easy enough for someone without daughters to say so, but the princess realized that in the process of getting to know each other her daughter might fall in love — and fall in love with someone who did not care to marry her, or who was completely unfit to be her husband. And however much she was told that in our times young people ought to arrange their own lives, she could not bring herself to believe it, just as she could not have believed that, in any age, the most suitable plaything for a five-year-old was a loaded pistol. So the princess was more uneasy over Kitty than she had been over her older sisters.

Now her fear was that Vronsky might confine himself to merely flirting with her daughter. She could see that her daughter was in love with him, and tried to comfort herself with the thought that he was an honorable man and would not do such a thing. But at the same time she knew how easy it is, with the loose manners of today, to turn a girl's head, and how lightly men in general regard that kind of offense. The week before, Kitty had told her mother about a conversation she had had with Vronsky during a mazurka. The conversation had partly reassured the princess; but completely at ease she could not be. Vronsky had told Kitty that both he and his brother were so used to obeying their mother that they never made up their minds to anything important without consulting her. "And just now I am impatiently waiting for my mother's arrival from Petersburg as something particularly fortunate," he had told her.

Kitty had repeated this without attaching any significance to it. But her mother had seen it differently. She knew that the old lady was expected any day now, that she would be pleased at her son's choice, and she found it strange that he should not make his offer for fear of vexing his mother. Still, she was so anxious to see the marriage made, and even more so to be free of her fears, that she chose to believe it. Bitter as it was for the princess to see the unhappiness of her eldest daughter, Dolly, on the point of leaving her husband, her anxiety over the resolution of her youngest daughter's fate absorbed all her feelings. Today, with Levin's reappearance, a fresh source of worry had opened up. She was afraid her daughter — who at one time, she had imagined, had a feeling for Levin — might, out of an excessive sense of honor, refuse Vronsky, and that Levin's arrival might generally complicate and delay the matter that had been so close to being settled.
"Now — has he been here long?" the princess asked about Levin as they returned home.
"He arrived today, mamma."
"There's one thing I want to say..." the princess began, and from her serious, watchful face Kitty guessed what was coming.
"Mamma," she said, flushing hotly and turning quickly to her, "please, please don't say anything about that. I know — I know all about it."
She wanted the same thing her mother wanted, but the reasons behind her mother's wishes wounded her.
"I only want to say that to raise hopes..."
"Mamma, darling, for goodness' sake, don't talk about it. It's so horrible to talk about it."
"All right, I won't," her mother said, seeing the tears in her daughter's eyes; "but one thing, my love — you promised me you'd keep no secrets from me. You won't, will you?"

"Never, mamma, no secrets," answered Kitty, flushing slightly and looking her mother straight in the face. "But there's nothing for me to tell you, and I... I... even if I wanted to, I wouldn't know what to say or how... I don't know..."

"No, she could not tell a lie with those eyes," the mother thought, smiling at her agitation and her happiness. The princess smiled to see that what was going on in her soul at that moment seemed to the poor child so enormous and so important.

title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: After dinner, and right up to the beginning of the evening, Kitty was feeling something like what a young man feels before a battle. Her heart was pounding violently, and her thoughts could not settle on anything.

She felt that this evening, when the two of them would meet for the first time, would be a turning point in her life. And she kept picturing them to herself, sometimes each one separately, sometimes both together. When she thought of the past, she lingered with pleasure, with tenderness, over the memories of her relationship with Levin. The memories of childhood and of Levin's friendship with her dead brother gave a special poetic charm to her relations with him. His love for her, of which she was certain, was flattering and delightful to her, and it was pleasant for her to think about Levin. In her memories of Vronsky there was always a certain awkwardness, even though he was in the highest degree well-bred and at ease — as if there were some false note somewhere, not in Vronsky, who was very simple and nice, but in herself; whereas with Levin she felt perfectly simple and clear. But on the other hand, the moment she thought of the future with Vronsky, a vista of brilliant happiness opened up before her; with Levin the future seemed hazy.

When she went upstairs to dress and looked in the mirror, she noticed with delight that it was one of her good days, that she was in full command of all her powers — she needed this so badly for what was ahead. She was conscious of an outward composure and an easy grace in her movements.

At half-past seven she had only just come down into the drawing-room when the footman announced "Konstantin Dmitrievitch Levin." The princess was still in her room, and the prince had not come in. "So it is to be," Kitty thought, and all the blood seemed to rush to her heart. She was horrified by her own paleness as she glanced into the mirror. In that moment she knew beyond doubt that he had come early on purpose to find her alone and to propose. And only then, for the first time, did the whole thing present itself in a new light; only then did she realize that the question did not concern only her — with whom she would be happy, whom she loved — but that she was about to have to wound a man she liked. And to wound him cruelly. What for? Because he, the dear man, loved her, was in love with her. But there was no help for it; this had to be, and so it would be.

"My God! Am I really going to have to say it to him?" she thought. "Can I tell him I don't love him? That would be a lie. What am I supposed to say to him? That I love someone else? No, that's impossible. I'll go, I'll go."

She had reached the door when she heard his step. "No! It isn't honest. What do I have to be afraid of? I've done nothing wrong. Whatever has to happen, will happen! I'll tell the truth. And with him there's no being uneasy. There he is," she said to herself, seeing his powerful, shy figure with his shining eyes fixed on her. She looked straight into his face, as if begging him to spare her, and gave him her hand.

"It isn't time yet; I think I'm too early," he said, glancing round the empty drawing-room. When he saw that his expectations had been met — that there was nothing to keep him from speaking — his face went dark.
"Oh, no," said Kitty, and sat down at the table.
"But this was exactly what I wanted, to find you alone," he began, not sitting down and not looking at her, so as not to lose his nerve.
"Mamma will be down in a minute. She was very tired yesterday..."
She kept talking, not knowing what her lips were saying, not taking her pleading, caressing eyes off him.
He glanced at her; she blushed and stopped talking.
"I told you I didn't know whether I'd be here long... that it depended on you..."
She dropped her head lower and lower, not knowing herself what answer she would give to what was coming.

"That it depended on you," he repeated. "I meant to say... I meant to say... I came for this... will you be my wife?" he brought out, not knowing what he was saying; but feeling that the most terrible thing had been said, he stopped short and looked at her...

She was breathing heavily, not looking at him. She was feeling rapture. Her soul was flooded with happiness. She had never expected that the declaration of his love would have so powerful an effect on her. But it lasted only an instant. She remembered Vronsky. She raised her clear, truthful eyes, and seeing his desperate face, she answered hastily:
"That cannot be... forgive me."
A moment before, how close she had been to him, how important in his life! And how distant and remote she had become now!
"It had to be," he said, not looking at her.
He bowed and was about to retreat.

title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: But at that very moment the princess walked in. There was a look of horror on her face when she saw them alone and saw their disturbed expressions. Levin bowed to her and said nothing. Kitty did not speak or look up. "Thank God, she has refused him," the mother thought, and her face lit up with the habitual smile she greeted her Thursday guests with. She sat down and began questioning Levin about his life in the country. He sat down again as well, waiting for other visitors to arrive so that he could slip out unnoticed.
Five minutes later in came a friend of Kitty's, married the previous winter, Countess Nordston.

She was a thin, sallow, sickly, and nervous woman with brilliant black eyes. She was fond of Kitty, and her affection for her showed itself, as the affection of married women for girls always does, in the wish to make a match for Kitty after her own ideal of married happiness; she wanted her to marry Vronsky. Levin she had often met at the Shtcherbatskys' earlier in the winter, and she had always disliked him. Her unvarying favorite occupation when they met was poking fun at him.

"I do love it when he looks down on me from the height of his grandeur, or breaks off his learned conversation with me because I'm a fool, or is condescending. I love that — seeing him condescending! I'm so glad he can't bear me," she used to say of him.

She was right, for Levin really could not bear her, and despised her for what she was proud of and considered a fine trait — her nervousness, her delicate contempt and indifference for everything coarse and earthly.

Countess Nordston and Levin had fallen into the sort of relationship not infrequently seen in society, in which two people who remain outwardly on friendly terms despise each other so thoroughly that they cannot even take each other seriously, cannot even be offended by each other.
Countess Nordston pounced on Levin at once.

"Ah, Konstantin Dmitrievitch! So you've come back to our corrupt Babylon," she said, giving him her tiny yellow hand and recalling that he had happened to say earlier in the winter that Moscow was a Babylon. "Tell me, has Babylon been reformed, or have you degenerated?" she added, glancing at Kitty with a smirk.

"It's very flattering for me, countess, that you remember my words so well," Levin replied, having managed to recover his composure and from habit dropping at once into his tone of joking hostility toward Countess Nordston. "They must certainly make a great impression on you."
"Oh, I should think so. I always note them all down. Well, Kitty, have you been skating again?"

And she began talking to Kitty. Awkward as it would be for Levin to leave now, it would still have been easier than staying the whole evening and watching Kitty, who glanced at him every now and then and avoided his eyes. He was on the point of getting up when the princess, noticing that he was silent, addressed him.
"Will you be in Moscow long? But you're busy with the district council, aren't you, so you can't be away for long?"
"No, princess, I'm no longer a member of the council," he said. "I've come up for a few days."

"There's something the matter with him," Countess Nordston thought, glancing at his stern, serious face. "He's not in his old argumentative mood. But I'll draw him out. I do love making a fool of him in front of Kitty, and I will."

"Konstantin Dmitrievitch," she said to him, "do explain to me, please, what's the meaning of this. You know all about these things. At home in our village of Kaluga all the peasants and all the women have drunk up everything they had, and now they can't pay us any rent. What's the meaning of that? You're always praising the peasants so."
At that instant another lady came into the room, and Levin got up.
"Excuse me, countess, but I really know nothing about it and can't tell you anything," he said, and glanced at the officer who had come in behind the lady.

"That must be Vronsky," Levin thought, and to be sure of it he glanced at Kitty. She had already had time to look at Vronsky and was now glancing at Levin. And simply from the look in her eyes, which had grown unconsciously brighter, Levin knew that she loved that man, knew it as surely as if she had told him so in words. But what kind of man was he? Now, for better or worse, Levin could not help staying; he had to find out what the man she loved was like.

There are people who, on meeting a successful rival, no matter in what, are at once inclined to turn their backs on everything good in him and to see only what is bad. There are others, on the other hand, who want above all to find in that lucky rival the qualities by which he has outstripped them, and who go looking, with an aching heart, only for what is good. Levin belonged to the second sort. But he had no difficulty in finding what was good and attractive in Vronsky. It was obvious at first glance. Vronsky was a squarely built, dark-haired man, not very tall, with a good-humored, handsome, and unusually calm and resolute face. Everything about his face and figure, from his short-cropped black hair and freshly shaven chin to his loosely fitting, brand-new uniform, was simple and at the same time elegant. Making way for the lady who had just come in, Vronsky went up to the princess and then to Kitty.

As he came up to her, his beautiful eyes shone with a particularly tender light, and with a faint, happy, modestly triumphant smile (so it looked to Levin), he bowed carefully and respectfully over her, and reached out his small, broad hand.
Greeting and saying a few words to everyone, he sat down without once glancing at Levin, who had not taken his eyes off him.
"Let me introduce you," said the princess, indicating Levin. "Konstantin Dmitrievitch Levin, Count Alexey Kirillovitch Vronsky."
Vronsky got up and, looking cordially at Levin, shook his hand.
"I believe I was supposed to have dined with you this winter," he said, smiling his simple, open smile; "but you unexpectedly left for the country."
"Konstantin Dmitrievitch despises and hates town and us townspeople," said Countess Nordston.
"My words must make a deep impression on you, since you remember them so well," said Levin, and, suddenly aware that he had just said the same thing before, he reddened.
Vronsky looked at Levin and Countess Nordston and smiled.
"Are you always in the country?" he inquired. "I should think it must be dull in winter."
"It isn't dull if you have work to do; besides, one isn't dull alone," Levin replied curtly.
"I'm fond of the country," said Vronsky, noticing — and pretending not to notice — Levin's tone.
"But I hope, count, you wouldn't agree to live in the country always," said Countess Nordston.

"I don't know; I've never tried it for long. I had an odd feeling once," he went on. "I never longed so for the country, the Russian countryside, with bast shoes and peasants, as when I was spending a winter with my mother in Nice. Nice itself is dull enough, you know. And really, Naples and Sorrento are only pleasant for a short time. And it's just there that Russia comes back to me most vividly, and especially the country. It's as though..."
He kept talking, addressing both Kitty and Levin in turn, his serene, friendly eyes moving from one to the other, and clearly saying whatever happened to come into his head.
Noticing that Countess Nordston wanted to say something, he stopped short without finishing what he had begun and listened to her attentively.

The conversation did not flag for a moment, so that the princess, who always kept in reserve, in case the conversation should run out, two heavy guns — the relative merits of classical and modern education, and universal military service — did not have to bring out either of them, and Countess Nordston had no chance to tease Levin.
Levin wanted to join in the general conversation but could not; saying to himself every minute, "Now go," he still did not go, as though waiting for something.
The conversation turned to table-turning and spirits, and Countess Nordston, who believed in spiritualism, began describing the marvels she had seen.
"Ah, countess, you simply must take me — for pity's sake, do take me to see them. I've never seen anything out of the ordinary, though I'm always on the lookout," Vronsky said, smiling.
"Very well — next Saturday," Countess Nordston answered. "But you, Konstantin Dmitrievitch, do you believe in it?" she asked Levin.
"Why are you asking me? You know what I'll say."
"But I want to hear your opinion."

"My opinion," Levin answered, "is just that this table-turning simply proves that what is called educated society is no higher than the peasants. They believe in the evil eye, and in witchcraft and omens, while we..."
"Oh, so you don't believe in it?"
"I can't believe in it, countess."
"But if I've seen it myself?"
"The peasant women tell us they have seen goblins."
"So you think I'm lying?"
And she gave a mirthless laugh.

"Oh no, Masha, Konstantin Dmitrievitch said he couldn't believe in it," said Kitty, blushing for Levin; Levin saw this, and, still more exasperated, would have answered, but Vronsky, with his bright, open smile, rushed to the rescue of a conversation that was threatening to become unpleasant.
"You don't admit the possibility at all?" he asked. "Why not? We accept the existence of electricity, of which we know nothing. Why shouldn't there be some new force, still unknown to us, which..."

"When electricity was discovered," Levin cut in quickly, "only the phenomenon was discovered; what produced it and what its effects might be were unknown, and ages passed before any practical uses for it were thought of. But the spiritualists have started with tables writing for them and spirits appearing to them, and only afterwards begun to say that it is some unknown force."
Vronsky listened to Levin attentively, as he always did, obviously interested in what he was saying.

"Yes, but what the spiritualists say is: we don't yet know what this force is, but a force exists, and these are the conditions under which it acts. Let the scientists work out what the force consists of. No, I don't see why a new force shouldn't exist, if it..."

"Because with electricity," Levin interrupted again, "every time you rub tar against wool, a recognized phenomenon appears, but in this case it doesn't happen every time, and so it isn't a natural phenomenon at all."

Feeling, presumably, that the conversation was taking too serious a tone for a drawing-room, Vronsky offered no rejoinder, but, by way of trying to change the subject, smiled brightly and turned to the ladies.
"Let's try it right now, countess," he said; but Levin meant to finish saying what he thought.

"I think," he went on, "that this attempt by the spiritualists to explain their wonders as some new natural force is utterly pointless. They boldly talk of spiritual force, and then try to subject it to material experiment."
Everyone was waiting for him to finish, and he felt it.
"And I think you would be a first-rate medium," said Countess Nordston; "there's something enthusiastic in you."
Levin opened his mouth, was about to say something, reddened, and said nothing.
"Let's try table-turning right now, please," Vronsky said. "Princess, will you allow it?"
And Vronsky stood up, looking for a small table.

Kitty got up to fetch a table, and as she passed her eyes met Levin's. She felt for him with her whole heart, the more so because she was pitying him for suffering of which she herself was the cause. "If you can forgive me, forgive me," her eyes said; "I am so happy."

"I hate them all, and you, and myself," his eyes answered, and he picked up his hat. But he was not to escape. Just as they were arranging themselves around the table, and Levin was on the point of leaving, the old prince came in, and after greeting the ladies turned to Levin.

"Ah!" he began with delight. "Been here long, my boy? I didn't even know you were in town. Very glad to see you." The old prince embraced Levin, and while talking to him did not notice Vronsky, who had risen and was waiting calmly for the prince to turn to him.

Kitty felt how distasteful her father's warmth was to Levin after what had just happened. She also saw how coldly her father at last acknowledged Vronsky's bow, and how Vronsky looked at her father with amiable bewilderment, as if trying and failing to understand how and why anyone could be hostile toward him, and she flushed.
"Prince, let us have Konstantin Dmitrievitch," said Countess Nordston; "we want to try an experiment."

"What experiment? Table-turning? Well, you must excuse me, ladies and gentlemen, but to my mind it's better fun to play the ring game," said the old prince, looking at Vronsky and guessing that the idea had been his. "There's some sense in that, at least."
Vronsky looked at the prince in surprise with his resolute eyes and, with a faint smile, at once began talking to Countess Nordston about the great ball that was coming up next week.

"I hope you'll be there?" he said to Kitty. As soon as the old prince turned away from him, Levin slipped out unnoticed, and the last impression he carried away of that evening was the smiling, happy face of Kitty answering Vronsky's question about the ball.

title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: At the end of the evening Kitty told her mother about her conversation with Levin, and despite all the pity she felt for him, she was glad at the thought that she had received an _offer_. She had no doubt that she had acted rightly. But after she had gone to bed, for a long time she could not sleep. One impression followed her relentlessly. It was Levin's face, his scowling brows and his kind eyes looking out in dark dejection beneath them, as he stood listening to her father and glancing at her and at Vronsky. And she felt so sorry for him that tears came to her eyes. But immediately she thought of the man for whom she had given him up. She vividly recalled his manly, resolute face, his noble self-possession, the good nature that showed in everything he did toward everyone. She remembered the love of the man she loved, and once more all was joy in her soul, and she lay on the pillow smiling with happiness. "I'm sorry, I'm sorry; but what could I do? It's not my fault," she said to herself; but an inner voice told her something else. Whether she felt remorse for having won Levin's love or for having refused him, she could not tell. But her happiness was poisoned by doubts. "Lord, have mercy on us; Lord, have mercy on us; Lord, have mercy on us!" she repeated to herself until she fell asleep.
Meanwhile downstairs, in the prince's little library, one of those scenes that so often took place between the parents about their favorite daughter was unfolding.

"What? I'll tell you what!" the prince shouted, waving his arms and once again wrapping his squirrel-lined dressing-gown around him. "That you've no pride, no dignity; that you're disgracing your daughter, ruining her, with this vulgar, stupid matchmaking!"
"But really, for mercy's sake, prince, what have I done?" said the princess, almost in tears.

She, pleased and happy after the conversation with her daughter, had gone in to the prince to say good-night as usual, and although she had no intention of telling him about Levin's offer and Kitty's refusal, she nonetheless hinted to her husband that she thought things were practically settled with Vronsky and that he would declare himself as soon as his mother arrived. And at those words the prince had at once flown into a rage and begun to use unseemly language.

"What have you done? I'll tell you what. First of all, you're trying to land an eligible gentleman, and all Moscow will be talking about it, and with good reason. If you have evening parties, invite everyone — don't pick out the possible suitors. Invite all the young bucks. Hire a piano player and let them dance, not the way you do things these days, hunting for good matches. It makes me sick, sick to see it, and you've gone on with it until you've turned the poor girl's head. Levin is a thousand times the better man. As for this little Petersburg dandy, they're turned out by the machine, all on one pattern, all precious rubbish. But even if he were a prince of the blood, my daughter need not run after anyone."
"But what have I done?"
"Why, you've..." the prince shouted angrily.
"I know that if one were to listen to you," the princess cut in, "we'd never marry our daughter off. If that's how it's to be, we may as well move to the country."
"Well, and we'd better."
"But wait a minute. Am I trying to chase them down? I'm not trying to chase them down in the least. A young man, and a very nice one, has fallen in love with her, and she, I think..."

"Oh yes, you think! And what if she really is in love and he's no more thinking of marriage than I am! Oh, that I should live to see it! Ah! Spiritualism! Ah! Nice! Ah! The ball!" And the prince, imagining he was mimicking his wife, made a mincing curtsey at each word. "And that's how we're preparing wretchedness for Kitty — and she really has got the notion into her head..."
"But what makes you suppose so?"

"I don't suppose; I know. We have eyes for such things, even if women don't. I can see a man who has serious intentions — that's Levin — and I can see a peacock, like this featherhead, who's only amusing himself."
"Oh, well, once you've got an idea into your head..."
"Well, you'll remember my words, but too late — just as with Dolly."
"All right, all right, we won't talk about it," the princess cut in, remembering her unlucky Dolly.
"By all means, and good-night!"
And making the sign of the cross over each other, husband and wife parted with a kiss, each still holding to his own opinion.

The princess had at first been quite sure that the evening had settled Kitty's future and that there could be no doubt about Vronsky's intentions, but her husband's words had unsettled her. And as she returned to her own room, in dread of the unknown future, she too, like Kitty, repeated several times in her heart, "Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy; Lord, have mercy."

title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Vronsky had never known anything like a real home life. His mother had been in her youth a brilliant society woman who had had during her marriage, and still more afterwards, many love affairs notorious throughout the fashionable world. His father he hardly remembered, and he had been educated in the Corps of Pages.

Leaving the school very young as a brilliant officer, he had at once entered the circle of wealthy Petersburg military men. Although he did go now and then into Petersburg society, his love affairs had always until now taken place outside it.

In Moscow, for the first time, after his luxurious and coarse Petersburg life, he had felt the whole charm of intimacy with a sweet and innocent girl of his own rank who cared for him. It never even crossed his mind that there could be anything wrong in his behavior toward Kitty. At balls he danced principally with her. He was a constant visitor at the house. He talked to her as people commonly talk in society — all sorts of nonsense, but nonsense to which he could not help attaching a special meaning in her case. Although he said nothing to her that he could not have said in front of everyone, he felt that she was becoming more and more dependent on him, and the more he felt this, the more he liked it, and the more tender his feeling for her grew. He did not know that his behavior toward Kitty had a definite name — that it was courting young girls with no intention of marriage, and that such courting was one of the bad practices common among brilliant young men like himself. It seemed to him that he was the first to have discovered this pleasure, and he was enjoying his discovery.

Had he been able to overhear what her parents were saying that evening — had he been able to step inside the family's perspective and learn that Kitty would be miserable if he did not marry her — he would have been thoroughly astonished, and wouldn't have believed it. He couldn't accept that something that gave such great and delicate pleasure to him, and above all to her, could be wrong. Still less could he have accepted that he ought to marry.

Marriage had never presented itself to him as a possibility. He not only disliked family life, but family, and especially a husband, was, according to the views general in the bachelor world in which he lived, conceived of as something alien, repulsive, and, above all, ridiculous.

But although Vronsky had not the slightest suspicion of what the parents were saying, he felt, on coming away from the Shtcherbatskys', that the secret spiritual bond between him and Kitty had grown so much stronger that evening that some step had to be taken. But what step could and should be taken, he could not imagine.

"What is so exquisite," he thought as he left the Shtcherbatskys', carrying away with him, as he always did, a delicious feeling of purity and freshness — partly because he had not been smoking for a whole evening — and with it a new feeling of tenderness at her love for him — "what is so exquisite is that not a word has been said by either of us, but we understand each other so well in this unseen language of looks and tones, that this evening more clearly than ever she told me she loves me. And how secretly, simply, and, above all, how trustfully. I feel better, purer. I feel I have a heart, and that there is a great deal of good in me. Those sweet, loving eyes! When she said: 'Indeed I do...'
"Well, what then? Oh, nothing. It's good for me, and good for her." And he started wondering where to finish the evening.

He ran through in his mind the places he might go. "Club? A game of bezique, champagne with Ignatov? No, I won't go. _Château des Fleurs_? I'll find Oblonsky there, songs, the cancan. No, I'm sick of it. That's why I like the Shtcherbatskys' — I'm growing better. I'll go home." He went straight to his room at Dussots' Hotel, ordered supper, undressed, and as soon as his head touched the pillow fell into a sound sleep.

title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The next day at eleven in the morning Vronsky drove to the Petersburg railway station to meet his mother, and the first person he ran into on the great flight of steps was Oblonsky, who was expecting his sister by the same train.
"Ah! Your excellency!" cried Oblonsky. "Whom are you meeting?"
"My mother," Vronsky answered, smiling, as everyone did who met Oblonsky. He shook hands with him, and together they climbed the steps. "She's supposed to arrive from Petersburg today."
"I was looking out for you till two o'clock last night. Where did you go after the Shtcherbatskys'?"
"Home," Vronsky answered. "I have to admit, I felt so content yesterday after the Shtcherbatskys' that I didn't feel like going anywhere."
"I know a gallant steed by tokens sure,
And by his eyes I know a youth in love,"
Stepan Arkadyevitch declaimed, exactly as he had done before to Levin.
Vronsky smiled with a look that seemed to say he did not deny it, but he quickly changed the subject.
"And whom are you meeting?" he asked.
"Me? I've come to meet a pretty woman," said Oblonsky.
"You don't say."
"_Honi soit qui mal y pense!_ My sister Anna."
"Ah — that's Madame Karenina," said Vronsky.
"You know her, no doubt?"
"I think I do. Or perhaps not... I'm really not sure," Vronsky answered absently, with a vague recollection of something stiff and tedious called up by the name Karenina.
"But Alexey Alexandrovitch, my celebrated brother-in-law — you surely must know him. The whole world knows him."
"I know him by reputation and by sight. I know he's clever, learned, somewhat religious... But you know that's not, _not in my line,_" said Vronsky in English.
"Yes, he's a very remarkable man — rather a conservative, but a splendid man," Stepan Arkadyevitch said. "A splendid man."
"Oh well, so much the better for him," Vronsky said, smiling. "Ah, you've come," he said to a tall old footman of his mother's who was standing at the door; "come here."
Beyond the general charm Oblonsky had for everyone, Vronsky had lately felt himself particularly drawn to him because in his imagination he was bound up with Kitty.
"Well, what about it — shall we put on a supper Sunday for the _diva?_" he asked, smiling and taking his arm.
"Of course. I'm collecting subscriptions. Oh, did you meet my friend Levin?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked.
"Yes; but he left rather early."
"He's a capital fellow," Oblonsky went on. "Isn't he?"

"I don't know why it is," Vronsky answered, "with all Moscow people — present company excepted, of course," he put in jokingly, "there's something uncompromising. They're all on the defensive, lose their tempers, as if they all want to make you feel something..."
"Yes, that's true, it is so," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, laughing good-humoredly.
"Will the train be in soon?" Vronsky asked a railway official.
"The train's been signaled," the man answered.

The train's approach was made more and more evident by the preparatory bustle in the station, the rush of porters, the movement of policemen and attendants, and people there to meet it. Through the frosty haze workmen in short sheepskin coats and soft felt boots could be seen crossing the rails of the curving line. The hiss of the boiler could be heard on the distant rails, and the rumble of something heavy.

"No," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, who felt a strong urge to tell Vronsky about Levin's intentions toward Kitty. "No, you haven't got the right impression of Levin. He's a very nervous man, and sometimes out of sorts, it's true; but at other times he's very nice. He's a true, honest nature, and a heart of gold. But yesterday there were special reasons," Stepan Arkadyevitch went on with a meaningful smile, completely forgetting the genuine sympathy he had felt the day before for his friend and feeling that same sympathy now, only for Vronsky. "Yes, there were reasons why he couldn't help being either particularly happy or particularly unhappy."
Vronsky stopped and asked directly, "How so? Do you mean he proposed to your _belle-sœur_ yesterday?"

"Maybe," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "I had an idea of something of the kind yesterday. Yes, if he left early and was out of sorts too, that must mean it... He's been in love so long, and I'm very sorry for him."

"So that's it. I should imagine, though, she might count on a better match," said Vronsky, straightening up and pacing again. "Though of course I don't know him," he added. "Yes, that's a hateful position. That's why most fellows prefer to deal with Klaras. If you don't succeed with that sort it only proves you don't have enough cash, but in this case one's dignity is at stake. But here's the train."

The engine had already whistled in the distance. A few moments later the platform was trembling, and with puffs of steam hanging low in the frosty air, the engine rolled up, the lever of its middle wheel moving rhythmically up and down, and the stooping figure of the engine-driver covered in frost. Behind the tender, setting the platform swaying more and more slowly, came the luggage van with a dog whining inside. At last the passenger carriages rolled in, rocking before they came to a stop.

A smart guard jumped out, blowing his whistle, and after him, one by one, the impatient passengers began to step down: an officer of the guards, holding himself erect and looking around severely; a nimble little merchant with a satchel, smiling cheerfully; a peasant with a sack over his shoulder.

Vronsky, standing beside Oblonsky, watched the carriages and the passengers, completely forgetting his mother. What he had just heard about Kitty excited and delighted him. Without realizing it, he squared his chest and his eyes flashed. He felt himself a conqueror.
"Countess Vronskaya is in that compartment," said the smart guard, coming up to Vronsky.

The guard's words roused him and forced him to think of his mother and the coming meeting with her. In his heart he did not respect his mother, and without admitting it to himself, he did not love her, though in keeping with the ideas of the set in which he lived and his own upbringing he could not have conceived of any behavior toward his mother that was not in the highest degree respectful and obedient — and the more outwardly obedient and respectful his behavior, the less in his heart he respected and loved her.

title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Vronsky followed the guard to the carriage, and at the compartment door he stopped short to let a lady get out.

With the instinct of a man of the world, from one glance at this lady's appearance Vronsky classified her as belonging to the best society. He begged pardon and was about to get into the carriage when he felt he had to glance at her once more — not because she was very beautiful, not on account of the elegance and modest grace that were apparent in her whole figure, but because in the expression of her charming face, as she passed close by him, there was something especially caressing and soft. As he looked round, she too turned her head. Her shining gray eyes, which looked dark from the thick lashes, rested with friendly attention on his face, as if she were recognizing him, and then promptly turned away to the passing crowd, as though looking for someone. In that brief look Vronsky had time to notice the suppressed eagerness that played across her face and flickered between her brilliant eyes and the faint smile curving her red lips. It was as if her nature were so brimming over with something that against her will it showed itself now in the flash of her eyes, now in her smile. She deliberately shrouded the light in her eyes, but it shone against her will in that faintly perceptible smile.

Vronsky stepped into the carriage. His mother, a dried-up old lady with black eyes and ringlets, screwed up her eyes, looking her son over, and smiled slightly with her thin lips. Getting up from her seat and handing her maid a bag, she gave her son her little wrinkled hand to kiss, and lifting his head from her hand, kissed him on the cheek.
"You got my telegram? Quite well? Thank God."
"You had a good journey?" her son said, sitting down beside her and listening in spite of himself to a woman's voice outside the door. He knew it was the voice of the lady he had met at the door.
"All the same, I don't agree with you," the lady's voice was saying.
"It's the Petersburg view, madame."
"Not Petersburg, simply feminine," she replied.
"Well, well, let me kiss your hand."
"Good-bye, Ivan Petrovitch. And could you check whether my brother is here and send him to me?" said the lady from the doorway, and turned back into the compartment.
"Well, have you found your brother?" Countess Vronskaya said to the lady.
Vronsky now understood that this was Madame Karenina.
"Your brother is here," he said, standing up. "Excuse me, I didn't recognize you, and, indeed, our acquaintance was so brief," Vronsky said, bowing, "that no doubt you don't remember me."

"Oh, no," she said, "I should have known you because your mother and I have been talking, I think, of nothing but you the whole way." As she spoke she let the eagerness that insisted on showing itself break through in her smile. "And still no sign of my brother."
"Do call him, Alexey," said the old countess. Vronsky stepped out onto the platform and shouted:
"Oblonsky! Here!"

But Madame Karenina did not wait for her brother; catching sight of him, she stepped out with her light, decisive step. And as soon as her brother had reached her, with a gesture that struck Vronsky by its decision and its grace, she flung her left arm around his neck, drew him quickly to her, and kissed him warmly. Vronsky gazed, never taking his eyes off her, and smiled, he could not have said why. But remembering that his mother was waiting for him, he went back into the carriage.

"She's very sweet, isn't she?" said the countess of Madame Karenina. "Her husband put her in with me, and I was delighted to have her. We talked the whole way. And so you, I hear... _vous filez le parfait amour. Tant mieux, mon cher, tant mieux._"
"I don't know what you're referring to, maman," he answered coldly. "Come, maman, let's go."
Madame Karenina came back into the carriage to say good-bye to the countess.
"Well, countess, you've met your son and I my brother," she said. "And my gossip is all used up. I'd have nothing else to tell you now."

"Oh, no," the countess said, taking her hand. "I could travel right around the world with you and never be bored. You're one of those delightful women in whose company it's lovely to be silent as well as to talk. Now, please, don't fret over your son — you can't expect never to be parted."
Madame Karenina stood quite still, holding herself very straight, her eyes smiling.
"Anna Arkadyevna," the countess explained to her son, "has a little boy of eight, I believe, and she has never been parted from him before, and she keeps fretting over leaving him."
"Yes, the countess and I have been talking the whole time, I about my son and she about hers," said Madame Karenina, and again a smile lit up her face — a caressing smile meant for him.

"I'm afraid you must have been horribly bored," he said, picking up at once the little ball of flirtation she had tossed him. But evidently she did not care to pursue the conversation in that vein, and she turned to the old countess.
"Thank you so much. The time has passed so quickly. Good-bye, countess."
"Good-bye, my love," the countess answered. "Let me have a kiss of your pretty face. I speak plainly, at my age, and I tell you simply that I've lost my heart to you."

Stereotyped as the phrase was, Madame Karenina obviously believed it and was delighted by it. She flushed, bent down slightly, and pressed her cheek to the countess's lips, drew herself up again, and with the same smile fluttering between her lips and her eyes, gave her hand to Vronsky. He pressed the little hand she gave him, and was delighted, as if at something special, by the energetic squeeze with which she freely and vigorously shook his hand. She left with the rapid step that carried her rather fully developed figure with such strange lightness.
"Very charming," the countess said.

That was exactly what her son was thinking. His eyes followed her until her graceful figure was out of sight, and even then the smile stayed on his face. He saw through the window how she went up to her brother, slipped her arm through his, and began telling him something eagerly — obviously something that had nothing to do with him, Vronsky — and at that he felt annoyed.
"Well, maman, are you perfectly well?" he asked again, turning to his mother.
"Everything was delightful. Alexander was very good, and Marie has grown very pretty. She's very interesting."
And she began once more on the subject that most interested her — the christening of her grandson, which had kept her in Petersburg, and the special favor the Tsar had shown her elder son.
"Here's Lavrenty," said Vronsky, looking out of the window; "now we can go, if you like."
The old butler who had traveled with the countess came over to announce that everything was ready, and the countess rose to leave.
"Come — there's not such a crowd now," said Vronsky.

The maid took a handbag and the lap dog, the butler and a porter the rest of the luggage. Vronsky gave his mother his arm; but just as they were getting out of the carriage several men ran past with panic-stricken faces. The station-master ran by too in his oddly colored cap. Obviously something unusual had happened. The crowd who had left the train were running back.

"What?... What?... Where?... Threw himself!... Crushed!..." could be heard in the crowd. Stepan Arkadyevitch, with his sister on his arm, turned back. They too looked frightened and stopped at the carriage door to avoid the crowd.
The ladies got in, while Vronsky and Stepan Arkadyevitch followed the crowd to find out the details of the disaster.
A guard, either drunk or too heavily muffled up against the bitter frost, had not heard the train backing up and had been crushed.
Before Vronsky and Oblonsky came back, the ladies had heard the facts from the butler.
Oblonsky and Vronsky had both seen the mutilated body. Oblonsky was visibly shaken. He was frowning and seemed about to cry.
"Ah, how awful! Ah, Anna, if you had seen it! Ah, how awful!" he said.
Vronsky did not speak; his handsome face was serious but perfectly composed.

"Oh, if only you had seen it, countess," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "And his wife was right there... It was awful to see her — she threw herself onto the body. They say he was the sole support of a huge family. How awful!"
"Couldn't anything be done for her?" Madame Karenina said in an agitated whisper.
Vronsky glanced at her and at once got out of the carriage.
"I'll be right back, maman," he said, turning round in the doorway.

When he returned a few minutes later, Stepan Arkadyevitch was already in conversation with the countess about the new singer, while the countess was looking impatiently toward the door, waiting for her son.

"Now, let's be off," Vronsky said, coming in. They went out together. Vronsky walked in front with his mother. Behind came Madame Karenina with her brother. Just as they were leaving the station, the station-master overtook Vronsky.
"You gave my assistant two hundred roubles. Would you kindly say for whose benefit you intend the money?"
"For the widow," said Vronsky, shrugging. "I should have thought there was no need to ask."
"You gave that?" Oblonsky cried behind him, and, squeezing his sister's hand, he added, "Very nice, very nice! Isn't he a splendid fellow? Good-bye, countess."
And he and his sister stood waiting, looking for her maid.
When they came out, Vronsky's carriage had already driven away. People going in were still talking about what had happened.
"What a horrible death!" said a gentleman, passing by. "They say he was cut in two."
"On the contrary, I think it's the easiest — instantaneous," another observed.
"How is it they don't take proper precautions?" said a third.
Madame Karenina settled into the carriage, and Stepan Arkadyevitch saw with surprise that her lips were quivering and that she was struggling to hold back her tears.
"What is it, Anna?" he asked when they had driven a few hundred yards.
"It's an omen of evil," she said.
"What nonsense!" said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "You've arrived — that's the main thing. You can't imagine how much I'm counting on you."
"Have you known Vronsky long?" she asked.
"Yes. You know we're hoping he'll marry Kitty."

"Really?" Anna said softly. "Come now, let's talk about you," she added, tossing her head as if she would physically shake off something heavy weighing on her. "Let's talk about your affairs. I got your letter, and here I am."
"Yes, all my hopes are in you," said Stepan Arkadyevitch.
"Well, tell me all about it."
And Stepan Arkadyevitch began to tell his story.
On reaching home Oblonsky helped his sister out, sighed, pressed her hand, and set off for his office.

title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: When Anna walked into the room, Dolly was sitting in the little drawing-room with a fair-haired, plump little boy who was already like his father, giving him a lesson in French reading. As the boy read, he kept fidgeting and trying to tear off a button that was nearly off his jacket. His mother had taken his hand away from it several times, but the plump little hand kept going back to the button. His mother pulled the button off and put it in her pocket.

"Keep your hands still, Grisha," she said, and she took up her work, a coverlet she had been making for a long time. She always took it up at depressing moments, and now she was knitting at it nervously, fingers twitching, counting the stitches. Although she had sent word the day before to her husband that it was nothing to her whether his sister came or not, she had made everything ready for her arrival and was waiting for her sister-in-law with emotion.

Dolly was crushed by her sorrow, completely swallowed up by it. Still, she did not forget that Anna, her sister-in-law, was the wife of one of the most important people in Petersburg and a Petersburg _grande dame_. And thanks to this circumstance she did not carry out her threat to her husband — that is, she remembered that her sister-in-law was coming. "And, after all, Anna isn't in any way to blame," Dolly thought. "I know nothing but the very best of her, and I've seen nothing but kindness and affection from her toward myself." It was true that, as far as she could recall her impressions in Petersburg at the Karenins', she had not liked their household itself; there had been something artificial about the whole framework of their family life. "But why shouldn't I receive her? Only let her not take it into her head to console me!" Dolly thought. "All those consolations and counsels and Christian forgivenesses — I've thought them all over a thousand times, and they're no use."

All these days Dolly had been alone with the children. She did not want to talk about her sorrow, but with that sorrow in her heart she could not talk about anything outside it. She knew that one way or another she would tell Anna everything, and she was alternately glad at the thought of speaking freely and angry at the necessity of speaking of her humiliation to her, his sister, and of hearing her ready-made phrases of advice and comfort. She had been on the watch for her, glancing at her watch every minute, and, as so often happens, she missed the very minute her visitor arrived, so that she did not hear the bell.
Hearing a rustle of skirts and light steps at the door, she looked around, and her care-worn face involuntarily expressed not gladness but astonishment. She got up and embraced her sister-in-law.
"What, here already?" she said as she kissed her.
"Dolly, how glad I am to see you!"

"I'm glad too," said Dolly, smiling faintly, trying from the expression on Anna's face to make out whether she knew. "Most likely she knows," she thought, noticing the sympathy on Anna's face. "Well, come along, I'll take you to your room," she went on, trying to put off the moment of confidences as long as possible.
"Is this Grisha? Heavens, how he's grown!" said Anna; and kissing him, her eyes never leaving Dolly's, she stood there and flushed a little. "No, please, let's stay here."
She took off her kerchief and hat, snagging the hat on a lock of her thick black curls, then tossed her head and shook her hair loose.
"You're radiant with health and happiness!" Dolly said, almost with envy.

"I?... Yes," said Anna. "Merciful heavens, Tanya! You're the same age as my Seryozha," she added, turning to the little girl as she ran in. She took her in her arms and kissed her. "Delightful child, delightful! Show me them all."
She named them — remembering not just their names but their ages, months, characters, and illnesses — and Dolly could not help being touched by it.
"Very well, we'll go to them," she said. "It's a pity Vassya is asleep."
After seeing the children, they sat down together over coffee in the drawing-room, alone now. Anna took the tray, and then pushed it away from her.
"Dolly," she said, "he's told me."
Dolly looked coldly at Anna; she was waiting now for the conventional phrases of sympathy, but Anna said nothing of the kind.
"Dolly, dear," she said, "I don't want to speak for him to you, or to try to console you — that can't be done. But, darling, I am simply sorry — sorry from my heart for you."

Under the thick lashes of her shining eyes, tears suddenly glittered. She moved closer to her sister-in-law and took her hand in her firm little one. Dolly did not pull away, but her face did not lose its frigid expression. She said:
"To comfort me is impossible. Everything is lost after what has happened, everything is over!"
And the moment she had said this, her face suddenly softened. Anna lifted Dolly's wasted, thin hand, kissed it, and said:
"But, Dolly, what's to be done, what's to be done? How is it best to act in this awful position — that's what you have to think about."

"All's over, and there's nothing more," Dolly said. "And the worst of it, you see, is that I can't simply throw him off — there are the children, I'm bound. And I can't live with him; it's a torture for me to see him."
"Dolly, darling, he's spoken to me, but I want to hear it from you: tell me about it."
Dolly looked at her questioningly.
Sympathy and unfeigned love showed on Anna's face.

"Very well," she said all at once. "But I'll tell it from the beginning. You know how I was married. With the upbringing mamma gave us I was more than innocent, I was stupid. I knew nothing. They say men tell their wives about their former lives, but Stiva" — she corrected herself — "Stepan Arkadyevitch told me nothing. You'll hardly believe it, but until now I imagined that I was the only woman he had ever known. That's how I lived for eight years. You have to understand that I was so far from suspecting infidelity that I regarded it as impossible, and then — try to imagine it — with such ideas, suddenly to find out all the horror, all the loathsomeness... You have to try to understand me. To be completely convinced of one's happiness, and all at once..." Dolly went on, holding back her sobs, "to get a letter — his letter to his mistress, my governess. No, it's too awful!" She quickly pulled out her handkerchief and hid her face in it. "I can understand being carried away by feeling," she went on after a brief silence, "but to deceive me deliberately, slyly... and with whom? To go on being my husband together with her... it's awful! You can't understand..."
