"Oh yes, I understand! I understand! Dolly, dearest, I do understand," said Anna, pressing her hand.
"And do you imagine he realizes the full awfulness of my position?" Dolly went on. "Not in the slightest! He's happy and content."
"Oh, no!" Anna broke in quickly. "He's to be pitied — he's weighed down by remorse..."
"Is he capable of remorse?" Dolly cut in, gazing intently into her sister-in-law's face.

"Yes. I know him. I couldn't look at him without feeling sorry for him. We both know him. He's good-hearted, but he's proud, and now he's so humiliated. What touched me most..." (and here Anna guessed what would touch Dolly most) "he's tortured by two things: that he's ashamed for the children's sake, and that, loving you — yes, yes, loving you beyond everything on earth," she hurriedly cut off Dolly, who would have answered — "he has hurt you, pierced you to the heart. 'No, no, she cannot forgive me,' he keeps saying."
Dolly looked dreamily away past her sister-in-law as she listened.

"Yes, I can see that his position is awful — it's worse for the guilty than the innocent," she said, "if he feels that all the misery comes from his own fault. But how am I to forgive him, how am I to be his wife again after her? For me to live with him now would be torture, just because I love what I used to feel for him..."
And sobs cut off her words. But as if on purpose, each time she softened she began again to talk about what made her furious.

"She's young, you see, she's pretty," she went on. "Do you know, Anna, my youth and my looks are gone, taken by whom? By him and his children. I've worked for him, and everything I had has gone in his service, and now of course any fresh, vulgar creature has more charm for him. No doubt they talked about me together, or, worse, were silent. Do you understand?"
Again her eyes burned with hatred.

"And after all that he will tell me... What? Can I believe him? Never! No, everything is over, everything that was once my comfort, the reward for my work and my suffering... Would you believe it, I was teaching Grisha just now: once this was a joy to me, now it's a torture. What do I have to strive and toil for? Why are the children here? What's so awful is that all at once my heart has turned, and instead of love and tenderness I have nothing but hatred for him; yes, hatred. I could kill him."
"Darling Dolly, I understand, but don't torture yourself. You're so distressed, so overwrought, that you're seeing many things wrongly."
Dolly grew calmer, and for two minutes both were silent.
"What's to be done? Think for me, Anna, help me. I've thought it all over and I can see nothing."
Anna could think of nothing, but her heart responded instantly to every word, every change of expression on her sister-in-law's face.

"There's one thing I would say," Anna began. "I'm his sister, I know his character — that capacity for forgetting everything, everything" (she waved her hand before her forehead), "that capacity for being completely carried away, but also for completely repenting. He can't believe it, he can't understand now how he could have acted as he did."
"No; he understands, he understood!" Dolly cut in. "But I... you're forgetting me... does it make it any easier for me?"

"Wait a minute. When he told me, I'll admit, I didn't realize the full awfulness of your position. I saw only him, and that the family was broken up. I felt sorry for him, but after talking to you I see it, as a woman, quite differently. I see your agony, and I can't tell you how sorry I am for you. But, Dolly, darling, while I fully realize your suffering, there is one thing I don't know: I don't know... I don't know how much love there still is in your heart for him. You know that — whether there is enough for you to be able to forgive him. If there is, forgive him!"
"No," Dolly was beginning, but Anna cut her short, kissing her hand again.

"I know more of the world than you do," she said. "I know how men like Stiva see it. You said he talks about you with her. That never happened. Such men are unfaithful, but their home and their wife are sacred to them. Somehow these women are still looked on by them with contempt, and don't touch their feeling for their family. They draw a kind of line that can't be crossed between them and their families. I don't understand it, but it is so."
"Yes, but he has kissed her..."

"Dolly, hush, darling. I saw Stiva when he was in love with you. I remember the time when he came to me and cried, talking about you, and all the poetry and the loftiness of his feelings for you, and I know that the longer he lived with you the loftier you stood in his eyes. You know we used to laugh at him for putting in at every word, 'Dolly is a marvelous woman.' You've always been a divinity to him, and you are that still, and this hasn't been an infidelity of the heart..."
"But if it's repeated?"
"It can't be, as I see it..."
"Yes, but could you forgive it?"

"I don't know, I can't judge... Yes, I can," Anna said, thinking for a moment; and, grasping the situation in her thoughts and weighing it in her inner balance, she added, "Yes, I can, I can, I can. Yes, I could forgive it. I couldn't be the same, no; but I could forgive it, and forgive it as though it had never been, never been at all..."

"Oh, of course," Dolly broke in quickly, as if saying what she had thought more than once. "Otherwise it wouldn't be forgiveness. If one forgives, it has to be completely, completely. Come, let's go; I'll take you to your room," she said, getting up, and on the way she embraced Anna. "My dear, how glad I am you came. It has made things better, ever so much better."

title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: The whole of that day Anna spent at home — that is, at the Oblonskys' — and received no one, though some of her acquaintances had already heard of her arrival and came to call that same day. Anna spent the whole morning with Dolly and the children. She sent only a brief note to her brother to tell him that he must not fail to come home for dinner. "Come, God is merciful," she wrote.

Oblonsky did dine at home; the conversation was general, and his wife, in speaking to him, addressed him as "Stiva," as she had not done before. The same estrangement still remained in the relations of husband and wife, but there was no talk now of separation, and Stepan Arkadyevitch saw the possibility of explanation and reconciliation.

Right after dinner Kitty came in. She knew Anna Arkadyevna, but only very slightly, and she came to her sister's now with some trepidation at the prospect of meeting this fashionable Petersburg lady whom everyone spoke so highly of. But she made a favorable impression on Anna Arkadyevna — she saw that at once. Anna was unmistakably admiring her loveliness and her youth; before Kitty knew where she was she found herself not only under Anna's sway but in love with her, the way young girls do fall in love with older married women. Anna was not like a fashionable lady, nor like the mother of an eight-year-old boy. In the elasticity of her movements, the freshness and unflagging eagerness that lingered in her face and broke out in her smile and her glance, she would rather have passed for a girl of twenty, were it not for a serious and at times sorrowful look in her eyes that struck Kitty and drew her in. Kitty felt that Anna was perfectly simple and was concealing nothing, but that she had another, higher world of interests, inaccessible to her, complex and poetic.
After dinner, when Dolly went off to her own room, Anna got up quickly and went over to her brother, who was just lighting a cigar.
"Stiva," she said to him, winking gaily, crossing him and glancing toward the door, "go on, and God help you."
He put down the cigar, understanding her, and walked off through the doorway.

When Stepan Arkadyevitch had disappeared, she went back to the sofa where she had been sitting, surrounded by the children. Either because the children saw that their mother was fond of this aunt, or because they felt some special charm in her themselves, the two elder ones, and the younger ones following their lead, as children so often do, had been clinging to their new aunt since before dinner and would not leave her side. And it had become a sort of game among them to sit as close to her as they could, to touch her, hold her little hand, kiss it, play with her ring, or even touch the flounce of her skirt.
"Come, come — as we were sitting before," said Anna Arkadyevna, taking her place again.
And again Grisha poked his little face under her arm and nestled his head against her gown, beaming with pride and happiness.
"And when is your next ball?" she asked Kitty.
"Next week, and a splendid ball. One of those balls where you always enjoy yourself."
"Are there really balls where you always enjoy yourself?" Anna said with tender irony.
"It's strange, but there are. At the Bobrishtchevs' you always enjoy yourself, and at the Nikitins' too, while at the Mezhkovs' it's always dull. Haven't you noticed?"

"No, my dear, for me there are no balls now where one enjoys oneself," said Anna, and Kitty caught in her eyes that mysterious world that was not open to her. "For me there are some less dull and tiresome than others."
"How can _you_ be dull at a ball?"
"Why shouldn't _I_ be dull at a ball?" Anna asked.
Kitty realized that Anna knew what answer was coming.
"Because you always look nicer than anyone."
Anna had the faculty of blushing. She blushed a little and said:
"In the first place, that's never the case; and secondly, if it were, what difference would it make to me?"
"Are you going to this ball?" asked Kitty.
"I imagine there'll be no avoiding it. Here, take it," she said to Tanya, who was pulling the loose ring off her white, slender-tipped finger.
"I should be so glad if you go. I'd so love to see you at a ball."

"At any rate, if I do go, I'll comfort myself with the thought that it gives you pleasure... Grisha, don't pull my hair. It's untidy enough as it is," she said, putting up a straying lock that Grisha had been playing with.
"I picture you at the ball in lilac."

"And why in lilac, particularly?" asked Anna, smiling. "Now, children, run along, run along. Do you hear? Miss Hoole is calling you to tea," she said, peeling the children off her and sending them off to the dining-room.
"I know why you're pressing me to come to the ball. You're expecting a great deal from this ball, and you want everyone to be there to share in it."
"How did you know? Yes."

"Oh, what a happy time you're at," Anna went on. "I remember it, and I know that blue haze, like the mist on the mountains in Switzerland. That mist that covers everything in that blissful time when childhood is just ending, and out of that vast circle, happy and gay, there is a path growing narrower and narrower, and it is both delightful and frightening to step into the ballroom, bright and splendid though it is... Who hasn't been through it?"
Kitty smiled without speaking. "But how did she get through it? How I'd love to know her whole love story," she thought, remembering Alexey Alexandrovitch's unromantic appearance — her husband.
"I know a little. Stiva told me, and I congratulate you. I liked him so much," Anna went on. "I met Vronsky at the railway station."
"Oh, was he there?" Kitty asked, blushing. "What did Stiva tell you?"

"Stiva gossiped about it all. And I'd be so glad... I traveled yesterday with Vronsky's mother," she went on; "and his mother talked without a stop about him, he's her favorite. I know mothers are partial, but..."
"What did his mother tell you?"

"Oh, a great deal! And I know he's her favorite; still, you can see how chivalrous he is... Well, for instance, she told me that he had wanted to give up all his property to his brother, that he had done something extraordinary when he was quite a child, saved a woman out of the water. He's a hero, in fact," said Anna, smiling and remembering the two hundred roubles he had given at the station.

But she didn't tell Kitty about the two hundred roubles. For some reason it was unpleasant to her to think about it. She felt that there was something in it that had to do with her, something that ought not to have been.

"She pressed me very much to come and see her," Anna went on; "and I'll be glad to go to her tomorrow. Stiva is staying a long time in Dolly's room, thank God," Anna added, changing the subject, and getting up, Kitty thought, displeased about something.
"No, I'm first! No, me!" the children screamed, having finished their tea, as they came running back to their Aunt Anna.
"All together," said Anna, and ran laughing to meet them, and embraced and swung around the whole crowd of swarming children, who shrieked with delight.

title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: Dolly came out of her room for the grown-ups' tea. Stepan Arkadyevitch did not come out. He must have left his wife's room by the other door.
"I'm afraid you'll be cold upstairs," Dolly said, addressing Anna; "I want to move you downstairs, and we'll be closer to each other."
"Oh, please don't go to any trouble on my account," Anna answered, watching Dolly's face closely to try to make out whether there had been a reconciliation or not.
"It will be lighter for you here," answered her sister-in-law.
"I assure you, I sleep anywhere, and always like a marmot."
"What's the question?" Stepan Arkadyevitch asked, coming out of his room and addressing his wife.
From his tone both Kitty and Anna knew that a reconciliation had taken place.
"I want to move Anna downstairs, but we'll have to hang up blinds. No one knows how to do it; I'll have to see to it myself," Dolly answered, addressing him.
"God knows whether they're fully reconciled," Anna thought, hearing her tone, cool and composed.
"Oh, nonsense, Dolly, always making difficulties," answered her husband. "Come, I'll do it all, if you like..."
"Yes, they must be reconciled," thought Anna.

"I know how you do everything," Dolly answered. "You tell Matvey to do what can't be done, and then go off, leaving him to make a muddle of everything," and her habitual, teasing smile curved the corners of Dolly's lips as she spoke.
"Full, full reconciliation, full," Anna thought. "Thank God!" and, glad that she was the cause of it, she went up to Dolly and kissed her.
"Not at all. Why do you always look down on me and Matvey?" said Stepan Arkadyevitch, smiling almost imperceptibly, and addressing his wife.

The whole evening Dolly was, as always, a little teasing in her tone with her husband, while Stepan Arkadyevitch was happy and cheerful, but not so much as to seem to have forgotten his offense now that he was forgiven.

At half-past nine an especially joyful and pleasant family conversation around the tea-table at the Oblonskys' was broken up by an apparently simple incident. But this simple incident for some reason struck everyone as strange. Talking about common acquaintances in Petersburg, Anna got up quickly.
"She's in my album," she said; "and, by the way, I'll show you my Seryozha," she added, with a mother's smile of pride.

Towards ten o'clock, when she usually said good-night to her son and often, before going to a ball, put him to bed herself, she felt depressed at being so far from him; and whatever she was talking about, her thoughts kept returning to her curly-headed Seryozha. She longed to look at his photograph and talk about him. Seizing the first pretext, she got up, and with her light, decisive step she went for her album. The stairs up to her room came out on the landing of the great warm main staircase.
Just as she was leaving the drawing-room, a ring was heard in the hall.
"Who can that be?" said Dolly.
"It's early for me to be fetched, and for anyone else it's late," Kitty observed.

"Probably someone with papers for me," Stepan Arkadyevitch put in. As Anna was passing the top of the staircase, a servant was running up to announce the visitor, who was himself standing under a lamp. Anna, glancing down, recognized Vronsky at once, and a strange feeling of pleasure and at the same time of dread of something stirred in her heart. He was standing still, not taking off his coat, pulling something out of his pocket. At the moment she was directly facing the stairs, he raised his eyes, caught sight of her, and a shadow of embarrassment and dismay passed over his face. With a slight nod of her head she walked on, hearing behind her Stepan Arkadyevitch's loud voice calling him to come up, and the quiet, soft, composed voice of Vronsky refusing.

When Anna returned with the album, he was already gone, and Stepan Arkadyevitch was telling them that Vronsky had called to ask about the dinner they were giving the next day for a celebrity who had just arrived. "And nothing would induce him to come up. What a queer fellow he is!" Stepan Arkadyevitch added.

Kitty blushed. She thought that she was the only person who knew why he had come, and why he would not come up. "He has been at home," she thought, "and didn't find me, and thought I would be here, but he didn't come up because he thought it was late, and Anna is here."
They all looked at each other, said nothing, and began to look at Anna's album.

There was nothing exceptional or strange in a man calling at half past nine on a friend to ask details of a proposed dinner party and not coming in, but it seemed strange to all of them. Above all, it seemed strange and not right to Anna.
